en: BhG 3.1 Arjuna said:
O Janārdana, if you consider intelligence to be superior to action, then...
Why then, O Keśava, do you urge me toward this terrible deed? // 1 //
Śrīdhara:
Having perceived a discrepancy between Sāṅkhya and Yoga, for the sake of the bewildered Jiṣṇu,
the Karma-yoga is proclaimed here in order to dispel the distinction between the two.
Thus, first, by the passage beginning with "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for" (Gītā 2.11), the discernment of the body from the Self was taught as a means to liberation.
Immediately thereafter, by the passage beginning with "This wisdom has been declared to you according to Sāṅkhya; now hear this regarding Yoga" (Gītā 2.39), action was also taught.
However, the relationship of primary and secondary importance between these two was not clearly demonstrated.

In this regard, because the state of one who is endowed with wisdom (*buddhi-yukta*)—the one of steady discernment (*sthita-prajña*)—is described through such qualities as freedom from desire, restraint of the senses, and absence of egoism, and because it is concluded with praise in the words, "This, O Pārtha, is the Brahmic state" (Gītā 2.72), Arjuna, considering that the Blessed One intended the superiority of wisdom over action, said: "If wisdom is superior... (*jyāyasī cet*).

If you consider the intellect to be superior—meaning more excellent and more conducive to liberation than action—then for what reason do you repeatedly urge me toward terrible, violent action by saying "fight" and "arise"? Why do you engage me in such a task? //1//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, having been introduced by the first chapter, the entire subject matter of the scripture has been summarized in the second chapter.
For instance: first, there is steadfastness in action performed without desire for fruit.
From that comes the purification of the internal organ;
from that, the renunciation of all actions preceded by the means such as tranquility and self-control;
and from that, steadfast devotion to the Blessed Lord accompanied by inquiry into the statements of the Vedānta.

Then follows the culmination in the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) and its fruit: liberation while living (jīvan-mukti) through the cessation of ignorance consisting of the three qualities (triguṇātmaka-avidyā), lasting until the exhaustion of the fruits of prārabdha-karma; and at the end of that, disembodied liberation (videha-mukti).

During the state of jīvan-mukti, one should adopt the divine endowment (daiva-sampad)—known as auspicious latent impressions (śubha-vāsanā)—which is conducive to the attainment of supreme detachment by taking recourse to the highest human goal. As for the demonic endowment (āsura-sampad), which is of the nature of passion (rājasī) and darkness (tāmasī), it is to be abandoned. Thus, through this distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, the entire meaning of the scripture is fully concluded.

Therein, the steadfastness in action without desire—which was introduced by the aphorism "Established in yoga, perform actions" (Gītā 2.48) and which serves as the means for purifying the mind—is elaborated in detail through its general and specific forms in the third and fourth chapters. Following that, for one whose internal organ is purified, there is the renunciation of desires preceded by the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*). Whoever...

The steadfastness in the renunciation of all actions, which was introduced by the verse beginning with "sarvān" (Gītā 2.71), has been explained in both concise and detailed forms through the fifth and sixth chapters.
By this much, the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou") has also been determined.

Then, by means of the six chapters beginning with [Gītā 2.61], "Therefore, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me, accompanied by inquiry into the words of Vedānta," the steadfast devotion (*bhakti*) to the Blessed Lord—enunciated in various ways—is expounded;
and by that much, the referent of the word *tat* (That) is also defined.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate in each respective place the internal connection and the specific intermediate purpose for every chapter.

Then, the steadfastness in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānaniṣṭhā*), which consists in the knowledge of the identity of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* and was indicated by the aphorism "He who does not perish, who is eternal" (Gītā 2.21) and so forth, is elaborated in the thirteenth chapter by means of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
And the fruit of this steadfastness in knowledge is stated as: "The Vedas have the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna" (Gītā 2.45).

The cessation of the three *guṇas*, which was indicated by the verse beginning with "Thus," is elaborated upon in the fourteenth chapter through the description of the characteristics of one who has transcended the *guṇas* (*guṇātīta*), as that very state is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

Furthermore, the culmination of supreme dispassion (*paravairāgya-niṣṭhā*), indicated by the verse beginning with "Then you shall go beyond detachment" (Gītā 2.52), is explained in the fifteenth chapter by way of the cutting down of the tree of *saṃsāra*.

And that which assists supreme dispassion, indicated by the characteristics of the one of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*) in the verse beginning with "With a mind undisturbed amidst sorrows" (Gītā 2.56), is likewise detailed.

The divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) is to be accepted, which was indicated by the verse beginning with "this flowery speech" (Gītā 2.42); likewise, the demonic endowment (*āsuryī saṃpat*), which is its opposite, is to be abandoned as described in the sixteenth chapter. Furthermore, the uncommon cause of the divine endowment is sattvic faith (*sāttvikī śraddhā*), which was indicated by the verse beginning with "free from the pairs of opposites, ever established in purity" (Gītā 2.45).
In the seventeenth chapter, by means of avoiding that which is opposed to it, the culmination of knowledge along with its fruit is thus established through these five chapters.
And in the eighteenth chapter, there is a summary of everything previously stated; such is the systematic connection of the entire meaning of the Gītā.

In that regard, in the preceding chapter, the Lord spoke of steadfastness in knowledge by relying on the Sāṅkhya perspective, beginning with: "This wisdom has been declared to you according to Sāṅkhya" (Gītā 2.39). Likewise, by relying on the Yoga perspective, he spoke of steadfastness in action, starting from "But as for Yoga, listen to this," and continuing until the end with: "Your right is to action alone... let there be no attachment to inaction" (Gītā 2.47).
Nor has the Lord clearly taught a distinction between the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) for these two culminations (*niṣṭhā*).
Nor should it be argued that both have the same qualified practitioner because their conjunction is intended;
for in the verse, "Action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya" (Gītā 2.49), the culmination in action is declared to be inferior in comparison to the culmination in wisdom.
Furthermore, in the verse "Whatever purpose there may be in a reservoir" (Gītā 2.46), it is shown that all fruits of action are included within the fruit of knowledge;

and after describing the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established, the conclusion is drawn regarding the fruit of knowledge with praise in the words "This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha" (Gītā 2.72); and in the passage beginning "That which is night for all beings" (Gītā 2.69), it is stated that because the knower lacks the perception of duality, the performance of ritual action is impossible.
For it is conceived, in accordance with worldly convention, that knowledge alone is the means to the fruit of liberation characterized by the cessation of ignorance;
and because of the Vedic scripture: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the attainment of the goal" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).
Now, if that is so, since knowledge and action—being as opposed as light and darkness—cannot be combined, let it be that they belong to different classes of qualified aspirants.
True;
it is not possible in this way, for it is not appropriate to give both instructions to a single Arjuna.
Indeed, it is not fitting to instruct one who is qualified for action in steadfastness in knowledge, nor is it fitting to instruct one who is qualified for knowledge in steadfastness in action.

If it is argued that both [the superior and inferior] are taught with respect to one and the same thing through conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), we say no; for conceptual differentiation between the superior and the inferior is untenable,
and because gradation is impossible in liberation, which is the true nature of the self characterized by the cessation of ignorance.

Therefore, since it is impossible to provide instruction for both [paths] if knowledge and action have different qualifications, and because their combination is impossible if they have the same qualification due to their mutual contradiction, and because the excellence of knowledge in relation to action would be untenable; furthermore, if an option between them were accepted,
one would abandon the superior knowledge— which is accomplished without effort— and instead perform the inferior action, which involves much exertion.
Thinking it to be improper, his mind becoming agitated,
Arjuna said: "If [action] is superior," O Janārdana.

The intention behind the address is this: "Since you are one who is entreated by all people to fulfill their own desires, it is not at all improper that I too am entreating you for the sake of determining what is most beneficial. Furthermore, if you consider the intellect directed toward the reality of the Self to be superior—that is, more praiseworthy—than even desireless action, then why do you enjoin me, your devoted follower, to this terrible action which abounds in many hardships such as violence?
With the words "Your right is to action alone" and so forth, You specifically urge me on.
O Keśava, Lord of All!

The intention is that it is not fitting for You—the Lord of All, the bestower of all desired things—to deceive one such as me, who has approached You with exclusive refuge through such pleas as "I am Your devotee," "I am Your disciple," and "Instruct me."
Viśvanātha:
Action performed without desire is elaborated upon in the third chapter;
furthermore, discernment regarding the conquest of desire and anger is also demonstrated.

Having perceived the superiority of the yoga of devotion that transcends the qualities (*guṇātīta-bhakti-yoga*), which brings about the state beyond the three qualities (*niṣtraiguṇya*)— as compared to the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) and the yoga of selfless action (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*) mentioned in the preceding verses— and manifesting his own longing for that very path, he addresses the Blessed One with the intimacy of a friend, urging him to engage in his own duty, the battle.
The higher, superior intellect is that which consists of resolute determination; the meaning is that it is devotion transcending the gunas.
Why do You urge me on, cause me to engage in this terrible action in the form of war? O Janardana, the meaning is that You afflict Your own people, Your kinsmen, by Your command.
And he says that no one is able to alter your command:
"O Keśava, who is Brahmā and who is Īśa, the Great God?
Even those two you bring under your control by your mere age. (1)
Baladeva:
In the third [chapter], disinterested action has been described in detail;
the means for conquering desire and the like, even that which is difficult to conquer, has also been shown.

In the preceding [section], the compassionate charioteer of Pārtha, desiring to uplift the world submerged in the mire of ignorance by means of instruction in the practice of self-knowledge, first taught the realization of the true nature of the individual soul— which is an auxiliary to that [knowledge]— and then, as a means to that end, taught desireless action performed without attachment.
This very same meaning is described for the sake of definitive determination through four chapters by means of different methods.
Among those, because the intellect of the individual self (*jīvātman*) is to be accomplished by means of action and intellect, the former is established as superior.
Regarding that, Arjuna asks: "Which is the greater? (*jyāyasī*).

If you consider that even for one free from desire, the realization of the individual self (*jīvātman*) is superior and more excellent because it is to be accomplished through action, then why do you enjoin me to that very attainment by engaging me in terrible action involving manifold exertions such as violence, saying "therefore, fight" and so forth?
Indeed, that realization which is the cause of the experience of the Self is to be accomplished by the cessation of the activity of all the senses; for that purpose—

The meaning is that only those things of its own kind, such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, would be appropriate, and not actions of a different kind consisting of the activities of all the sense organs. O Janārdana, you who are entreated by people seeking the highest good;
O Keśava, you who bring even Brahmā and Rudra under your control!
"Ka" is the name of Brahmā; I am the Lord of all embodied beings.
Since we two have arisen from your limbs, we therefore bear the name Keśava.
Thus ends Rudra’s speech to Kṛṣṇa in the *Harivaṃśa*. The sense is:
"Your command is difficult to transgress; you have been entreated by me, who seeks my own welfare. Having determined what is for my benefit, please speak. (1)
With these seemingly contradictory words, you appear to confuse my intellect.
Therefore, tell me with certainty that one path by which I may attain the highest good. (3.2)

Śrīdhara: Anticipating the objection that the excellence of action has indeed been stated in such passages as, "For there is nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war," he says: "By this confused [speech]... By that speech—which is confused, meaning it praises action in some places and knowledge in others, thus creating a doubt as it were—he seems to delude my intellect, making my mind oscillate between the two.
Therefore, having determined which one among these two is the better, speak;

or rather, having determined that this alone is the means for attaining the highest good—that by practicing which I may attain, or reach, the highest good, which is liberation—speak after having determined that single path alone. This is the meaning. //2//
Madhusūdana:
"Indeed, I do not deceive anyone, much less you, who are so very dear to me.
If you ask, 'Why then do you see any sign of deception in me?', he replies with the verse beginning with 'vyāmiśreṇa'."

Your speech is indeed not inconsistent for me; however, because of my doubt as to whether [the two paths] have the same subject matter or different subject matters, your statement—which presents to me the duality of steadfastness in knowledge and action—seems to me to be of confused meaning. Thus, you seem to delude my intellect—that is, my internal organ—because I, being of dull intellect, do not understand the intended purport of your words.
"You seem to join [them] through delusion.
Because you possess supreme compassion, you certainly do not cause delusion; rather, it is due to the defects of my own disposition that delusion arises—this is the meaning of the word "seem" (iva).

Since two contradictory things cannot be conjoined when they share a single substratum, and since an alternative (vikalpa) is untenable because they lack a single referent, [the sense is established].

If you think there is a difference in qualification based on what was said previously, then, since it is impossible to instruct me— being a single person— in two contradictory conclusions, determine for me whether that knowledge or action is the one and only qualification, and tell me.

"By which knowledge or action—spoken by You with the determination of the respective eligibility (*adhikāra-niścaya*) and performed by me—I might attain, or become fit to attain, the supreme good, which is liberation (*mokṣa*).

Thus, since neither an option (*vikalpa*) nor a combination (*samuccaya*) is possible when the two foundations of knowledge and action belong to a single eligible person (*ekādhikāritva*), it is established that Arjuna’s question is intended to discern the difference between the eligible persons. Here, all other erroneous views [of others] are [refuted].
This has already been refuted by the authority of Śruti, Smṛti, and logic; therefore,
since the author of the Commentary has already exerted great effort on this point again and again, I have not set out to do so here.
Perceiving the essence of the author of the Commentary’s thought, I here compose merely this treatise; the intention of the Blessed One is thereby made manifest.
Solely for the sake of purifying one's own speech. //2//
Viśvanātha:
O friend Arjuna,
it is true that devotion which transcends the qualities (guṇas) is indeed the most excellent of all.
However, because she is obtainable solely through the compassion of a spontaneous, exclusive, and great devotee, she is not something that can be accomplished by human effort alone.
Therefore, the blessing was simply given: "Become free from the three qualities; through my devotion which transcends the qualities, may you become free from the three qualities.
And when that blessing bears fruit, then you shall attain her, who is obtained through the grace of such a spontaneous and exclusive devotee.
If it is true that I have said, "But now, your right is to action alone," then why do you not decide upon action itself?
Why do you cast me into this ocean of doubt? To this he replies with the words beginning "by the confused... (vyāmiśreṇa).
In particular, by that speech which contains a thorough and complete mixture—a confluence of various meanings—you confuse my intellect; for instance:
"Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47), and "Being the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga" (Gītā 2.48).
"One endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds here;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in actions" (Gītā 2.50).
Thus, You speak even of knowledge as being denoted by the word "yoga."
When you say, "When your delusion-thicket [is destroyed]" (Gītā 2.52), you speak of knowledge alone.
Furthermore, what is the purpose here of the word *iva*? In reality, there is no admixture of multiple meanings in your statement, nor do you, being compassionate, have any desire to delude me.
The sense is that it is not the case that I am ignorant of those respective matters;
this is the hidden intention: action characterized by *sattva* is superior to action characterized by *rajas*, and that [superiority] belongs to the *sāttvika* alone.
Therefore, devotion devoid of qualities (nirguṇa-bhakti) is indeed the most excellent;
if you say that it cannot possibly exist in me,
then simply instruct me in pure (sāttvika) knowledge alone.
"May I be liberated from this very bondage of saṃsāra, which consists of suffering. //2//
Baladeva: Regarding the phrase "by means of what is mixed":

that statement which obstructs the relationship between the goal and the means—namely, the intellect of Sāṅkhya and the intellect of Yoga, both of which consist in the withdrawal of the senses—is called "mixed.
By such [a statement], you seem to delude my intellect.

In reality, however, there is no power to delude me in the Lord of All, who is my friend; it is solely due to a defect in my own intellect that I am driven so excessively by the meaning of words. Therefore, speak a single, unambiguous statement.

"Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone did they attain immortality; there is nothing uncreated [attained] by means of what is created"—according to such scriptural testimony, how may I determine what is to be practiced so that I might attain my own highest good? //2//
The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one, in this world a twofold path was declared by Me in the past.
For the followers of Sāṃkhya, it is by the yoga of knowledge; for the practitioners of Yoga, it is by the yoga of action. //3//
Śrīdhara: To this, the Blessed Lord spoke the reply beginning with "In this world" (*asmin loke*).
This is the meaning:
if I had taught two distinct paths of steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*)—consisting of action and knowledge—as independent means to liberation;
In that case, your question—"Tell me one of these two which is better"—would be appropriate;
however, I have not spoken in such a manner.
Only one single state of steadfastness in Brahman has been taught by both of them.

Since independence for those two, which exist in a relationship of subordinate and principal, is untenable, it is merely a difference in mode of a single [niṣṭhā] that has been described according to the distinction of qualified persons (adhikārin).
In this world, which is twofold due to the purity or impurity of the internal organ, there are two kinds of qualified persons;
that [niṣṭhā] which possesses these two modes was clearly declared by me, the omniscient one, in the previous chapter as the twofold niṣṭhā, which is devotion directed toward liberation.
He points out these two very methods with the words "by the yoga of knowledge," and so forth.

For the Sāṅkhyas— those of pure internal organs who have ascended to the stage of knowledge— the culmination, which is the state of Brahman, is said to be attained through the yoga of knowledge, such as meditation, for the sake of the ripening of knowledge.
"All these, having restrained, let him sit disciplined, intent on Me," and so forth; however,
for those yogins who desire to ascend to the stage of Sāṅkhya by means of the purification of the internal organ, and who are thus qualified for Karma-yoga as its preparatory means,
the steadfastness in Karma-yoga has been taught through such passages as, "For there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous battle."
Therefore, the final goal has been described as twofold according to the different stages of the purification of your mind:
"This wisdom regarding Sāṅkhya has been declared to you; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga. (3)
Madhusūdana:

When Arjuna had thus asked regarding the distinction between types of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*), the Blessed Lord spoke a reply corresponding to that in the verse beginning with "In this world" (*asmin loke*).

In this world—consisting of people considered to possess such qualifications—who are of two kinds due to the distinction between pure and impure internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there are two [types of] paths.

The two-fold culmination— consisting of devotion to knowledge and devotion to action— of one who is established [in yoga], which was previously declared by me, acting for your ultimate benefit, in the preceding chapter with full clarity;
thus, the intention is that you should not be weary on account of the doubt that the qualified practitioners are different.
By addressing him as "O sinless one," He indicates Arjuna’s fitness for instruction.

There is only one *niṣṭhā* (steadfastness), which is of two kinds according to the distinction between the states of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), but not two independent *niṣṭhās*; this is stated by using the singular form "niṣṭhā. As He will say: "He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, he truly sees" (Gītā 5.5).
He shows that very culmination in two ways with the words "Sāṅkhya" and so forth.

For those who have attained *saṅkhyā*—which is the correct knowledge of the Self—having renounced the world from the very time of their student life (*brahmacarya*), whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta, who have ascended to the plane of knowledge, and whose internal organs are purified; for these *sāṅkhyas*, it is by means of the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) that knowledge itself is joined.

The term *yoga* is derived from the etymology "that by which one is united with Brahman" (*brahmaṇāneneti*); through this, steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) has been described in such passages as, "Restraining all those [senses], let him sit disciplined, intent on Me" (Gītā 2.61).

However, for those yogins whose internal organs are impure and who have not yet ascended to the level of knowledge—namely, those yogins entitled to ritual action (*karmādhikāra-yogin*)—[steadfastness is attained] through the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*).
Yoga is defined by the etymology "that which is joined with the purification of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi-yoga*); steadfastness in that has been taught through such passages as,
"For there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war" (Gītā 2.31), for the purpose of ascending to the stages of knowledge by means of the purification of the internal organ.
Therefore, there is neither a combination nor an option between knowledge and action;

rather, for those whose internal organs are purified by desireless action, knowledge arises only through the renunciation of all actions. Thus, based on the distinction between the states of purity and impurity of the mind, two types of steadfastness have been taught to you, though they refer to one and the same goal.
"This wisdom has been declared to you in the context of Sāṃkhya; now hear this regarding Yoga" (Gītā 2.39).

Therefore, because both are useful for the same goal through the distinction of stages (*bhūmikā*), the intention is that there is no futility in the instruction even though the levels of qualification (*adhikāra*) differ.

To demonstrate this very point, it is said that for one whose mind is impure, the performance of action continues until the purification of the mind, but it is not the case that actions [are useless].
He demonstrates this through thirteen verses beginning with "Because of not undertaking... (Gītā 3.4) and ending with "He lives in vain" (Gītā 3.16).
Furthermore, he shows by means of two verses beginning with "But he who finds delight in the Self" (Gītā 3.17) that for the knower of pure mind, no action whatsoever is required.

Therefore, beginning with the words "one who is unattached," [the Lord] will demonstrate that even action, which is a cause of bondage, can become a cause of liberation through the gateway of the purification of the mind and the arising of knowledge, by means of skill characterized by the absence of desire for fruits.
Following that, however, having raised the question "Then by what?", He will show that action performed out of desire alone cannot be a cause of purity.

Therefore, by performing actions while indeed free from desire, you will become qualified for knowledge through the purification of the internal organ; thus the Blessed One will speak until the end of the chapter. //3//
Viśvanātha:
To this, the answer is as follows:
If I had taught karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga as means to liberation while they were indeed mutually independent of one another.

In that case, your question— "Tell me decisively which one of those two it is"— is appropriate. However, the twofold nature I have described— consisting of steadfastness in action and steadfastness in knowledge— is indeed due solely to the distinction between earlier and later stages.
But in reality, there is no duality of qualification with respect to liberation; thus he says in two verses beginning with "In the world.
"Twofold" means of two kinds; "niṣṭhā" means a firm state or a fixed limit.
It was "proclaimed aforetime," that is, stated in the previous chapter.

He explains that very point: for the Sāṅkhyas—those who possess *sāṅkha*, which is knowledge—their final goal (*niṣṭhā*) is attained through the yoga of knowledge alone; by that alone has their standard been established. The meaning is that in this world they are celebrated as knowers (*jñānin*), according to such passages as: "Restraining all those [senses], let him sit disciplined, intent on Me" (Gītā 2.61).

Likewise, for those yogis who, due to the absence of a purified inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), are unable to ascend to the plane of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*) but possess the means for such ascent, a steadfast practice (*niṣṭhā*) was established by way of *karma-yoga*—that is, through self-surrendered action free from desire (*niṣkāma-karman*).
The meaning is that they are indeed designated as "doers" (*karmin*), as stated in passages such as: "For there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war" (Gītā 2.31).
Thus, there is a twofold division merely by name into "the performers of action" (karmiṇaḥ) and "the possessors of knowledge" (jñāninaḥ).
In reality, however, it is the performers of action alone whose minds become purified through their actions and who thus become possessors of knowledge;
and it is the possessors of knowledge alone who are liberated through devotion—this is the intended meaning of the collection of my statements. //3//
Viśvanātha:
To this, the reply is as follows:
If I had stated that karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga are means for attaining liberation while being entirely independent of one another.

In that case, your question— "Tell me which one of those is it, having decided"— is appropriate. However, the twofold division I have described— namely, steadfastness in action and steadfastness in knowledge— is indeed based solely on the distinction between earlier and later stages.
But in reality, there is no duality of qualification regarding liberation; thus he says in two verses beginning with "In the world.
"Twofold" means of two kinds; "niṣṭhā" means a firm state or a fixed limit. It was "spoken of before," that is, declared in the previous chapter.
He explains that very point: for the Sāṅkhyas, there is the Sāṅkhya knowledge;

for those who possess it—who, by virtue of their purified internal organs (*antaḥ-karaṇa*), have ascended to the plane of knowledge—perfection is attained through the yoga of knowledge alone, and by that alone has the limit been established.
The meaning is that in this world they are renowned precisely as knowers, according to such passages as: "Restraining all these, let him sit disciplined, intent on Me" (Gītā 2.61).

Likewise, for those yogins who, due to the absence of purity of heart, are unable to ascend to the plane of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*) but possess the means for such ascent, a steadfast practice (*niṣṭhā*) has been established by way of *karma-yoga*—that is, through self-surrendered action free from desire—as a guiding rule (*maryādā*).
The meaning is that they are indeed designated as "doers" (*karmin*), as expressed in passages such as: "For there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war" (Gītā 2.31).
Thus, there is a twofold division merely by name into "those who perform action" (karmiṇaḥ) and "those who possess knowledge" (jñāninaḥ).
In reality, however, it is the very performers of action whose minds are purified by their actions that become possessors of knowledge;
and it is the possessors of knowledge alone who are liberated through devotion—this is the intended meaning of the collection of my statements. //3//
Baladeva: Thus questioned, the Blessed One said, "In this world... [and so forth].

O sinless one, O Pārtha of stainless intellect, although He knows the relationship of primary and subordinate qualities between the Sāṅkhya understanding (the path of knowledge) and the Karma understanding (the path of action)—just as there is a natural opposition between darkness and light—He speaks out of the doubt: "How can these two, being so contradictory, have a single person as their locus?"
The sense is that you ask because you have been prompted [by me].

In this world of people, which is twofold—consisting of those with pure minds and those with impure minds, and who are thus considered seekers of liberation—I, the Lord of All, have previously declared in the preceding chapter a twofold *niṣṭhā*, or steadfast abiding.

By using the singular form "one *niṣṭhā*," it is indicated that there is only one single goal (*ekātma-uddeśyatvāt*), and that while this one *niṣṭhā* is of two kinds due to the distinction between the two stages of the means and the end, there are not two separate *niṣṭhās*.
In this very way, he will state later: "The Sāṅkhya and Yoga are one" (Gītā 5.5).
He shows that steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) to be twofold with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
The first member of the compound *sāṅkhya-jñāna* is formed with the suffix *arha*.

The steadfast abiding of those possessing that [knowledge], namely the wise, through the yoga of knowledge has been described by such passages as, "When one abandons desires" (Gītā 2.55) and so forth; for "yoga" is indeed knowledge, according to the etymological derivation: "that by which one is joined (*yujyate*) with the Self.
The steadfast abiding of yogis who possess desireless action, through the yoga of action, has been described by such passages as, "Your right is to action alone" (Gītā 2.47) and so forth.
Action itself is yoga, based on the etymological derivation that "one is joined (*yujyate*) by means of this through the purification of the mind which has knowledge as its essence.
What is meant is this: a person seeking liberation does not indeed attain the culmination of knowledge—which has tranquility and other qualities as its limbs—at that very moment;

rather, it is only after having shaken off the impurities of the mind by means of action-yoga accompanied by right conduct. This is precisely what I stated previously in such passages as, "This path of the Sāṃkhya has been declared to you" (Gītā 2.39).
By not undertaking actions, a person does not attain freedom from action; nor does one achieve perfection merely through renunciation. (3.4)
Śrīdhara: Therefore, until the arising of knowledge through the complete purification of the mind, actions appropriate to one's caste and stage of life must be performed;
otherwise, because knowledge does not arise due to the absence of mental purity, he says "not by the non-commencement of actions.
By the non-commencement—that is, the non-performance—of actions, one does not attain, nor reach, *naiṣkarmya*, which is knowledge.

Now, one might object: "Since the Vedic scripture states that 'those desiring this very world renounce [the world],' and since this shows that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is a constituent part of liberation, liberation will result from renunciation alone;
what is the use of ritual actions?
Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Not so."
Without purification of the mind, one does not attain—that is, does not reach—success or liberation through renunciation alone that is devoid of knowledge. //4//
Madhusūdana:
Since an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause, he says, "not by rituals. Regarding this, it is said:
"By rituals—by the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by giving, and by austerity consisting of fasting—the Brahmins seek to know Him."

Thus, because of the Vedic injunction, a person who is turned outward and unfit for knowledge— due to the absence of mental purity resulting from the non-commencement and non-performance of those duties enjoined for the sake of self-knowledge— does not attain, that is to say, does not reach, *naiṣkarmya*, which is the state of being devoid of all action, namely, steadfastness through the yoga of knowledge.

[Objection: But surely, since the scripture states, "Desiring this very world, mendicants renounce," and since steadfastness in knowledge is established only through the renunciation of all action, what is the use of ritual acts? To this he says: "Nor does one attain perfection—characterized by steadfastness in knowledge and culminating in the complete fruit—merely by the act of renunciation alone, without the purification of the mind."
The meaning is that he does not attain it at all.
Without the purification of the mind produced by [prior] action, renunciation itself is not possible;
the point is that even if it is performed in some manner merely out of zeal, it does not culminate in its fruit. //4//
Viśvanātha:
He states that knowledge does not arise in the absence of purity of mind with the word "no.
Because of the non-commencement—that is, the non-performance—of scriptural actions, one who possesses an impure mind does not attain the state of actionlessness, which is knowledge.
"From renunciation" means from the abandonment of scriptural action. //4//

Baladeva: Therefore, he says in thirteen verses beginning with "Not by abstaining from actions" (*na karmaṇām*) that one whose mind is impure must perform only those very actions prescribed for oneself in order to purify the mind.

By the statement "from the non-commencement"—that is, the non-performance—of those actions which are prescribed as limbs of knowledge (by the words "this very [state]... through action"), a person of unpurified mind cannot attain *naiṣkarmya*, which is the cessation of all activity of the senses, meaning steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*).
He does not attain, nor does he obtain; and by the renunciation—that is, the abandonment—of those actions, he does not achieve perfection, which is liberation. //4//
For indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action; for everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of material nature. (3.5)
Śrīdhara: And the renunciation of actions consists merely in non-attachment toward them, but not in their abandonment by way of their own nature,
because that is impossible.
He says: "No one indeed.
At no time whatsoever, even for a single moment, does anyone—whether wise or ignorant—remain without performing action (*akarma-kṛt*), that is, without doing deeds.
The reason for this is: every person is impelled to action by the qualities (*guṇas*) such as attachment and aversion, which are born of *prakṛti* (nature) and arise from its inherent nature.
One is set into action by karma, being helpless and lacking self-mastery. //5//
Madhusūdana:
In that regard, one who lacks the purity born of action is turned outward;
for indeed, because of this, no one at any time, even for a moment, remains without performing action while their senses are unconquered.
Rather, he remains preoccupied solely with the performance of worldly and Vedic rituals; therefore, the meaning is that renunciation is not possible for one whose mind is impure.
Why, then, does the ignorant person not remain without performing actions?
Because (hi), for this reason.

Every living being, being devoid of purity of mind and lacking both necessity and self-mastery, is impelled toward action— whether worldly or Vedic— by the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas, which are born of nature, manifested from nature, or arise from one's own inherent disposition, such as passion, hatred, and the like.
Therefore, the meaning is that no one remains without performing actions.

Since the inherent qualities (guṇas) are the movers, for one whose intellect is impure—who always acts under the sway of others—renunciation of all actions is not possible; thus, the steadfastness in knowledge based on renunciation is not possible. This is the meaning. //5//
Viśvanātha:
However, one whose mind is impure, having taken up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), abandons scriptural action and sinks into worldly activity; thus he says, "For not... [na hi].
Now, is it not the case that renunciation itself is the obstacle to his engagement in Vedic and worldly actions?
Regarding this, he says: "By way of its effect. "Helpless" means lacking independence. //5//
Baladeva: He says "not indeed" (na hi) to show that one whose mind is impure, even after having renounced Vedic actions, sinks back into worldly activity.
If it is argued that renunciation itself is opposed to all action for such a person, he replies with the words "by necessity" (kāryataḥ):
[he acts] by means of the qualities born of nature (prakṛti), namely passion, hatred, and so forth, which arise from one's own disposition (svabhāva).
He is made to act; he is set in motion, being helpless and dependent on another. //5//
He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to dwell upon the objects of the senses with his mind, being deluded in soul, is called a hypocrite. (3.6)
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he censures the ignorant person who abandons action with the words "having restrained the organs of action" (karmendriyāṇi).
The organs of action are speech, hands, and so forth.

Having restrained them under the pretext of meditating on the Lord, such a person remains while recollecting the objects of the senses—the sense-objects—because his mind is unpurified and lacks steadiness in the Self.
The meaning is that such wrong conduct, being hypocritical behavior, is called "dāmbhika" (hypocrisy). //6//
Madhusūdana:
One who has renounced merely out of some kind of restless longing (*autsukya*) does not partake in the fruit thereof because his mind is impure;

for that deluded soul whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is corrupted by passion, hatred, and so forth, restrains and holds back the organs of action—speech, hands, and the rest—merely out of longing, yet continues to perform actions with the external senses.
This means:

one who, though having performed renunciation, remains with the conceit "I am a renunciant" and dwells recollecting in his mind sense objects such as sound—which are impelled by passion and the like—but not the reality of the Self, being devoid of action [only in appearance], is of false conduct; because of the absence of purity of being (*sattva-śuddhi*), he is unfit for the fruit and is therefore called one of sinful conduct.
Since renunciation of all actions has been prescribed here by the Śruti for the sake of discerning the meaning of the word "thou," one who abandons it would be fallen.
Thus, according to the Dharmaśāstra and other such texts, it is established that one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is not purified does not attain perfection merely through renunciation. //6//
Viśvanātha:
But surely there is some such renunciant;
is there not someone seen with eyes closed, devoid of the activity of the senses?

In this regard, it is said: he who, having restrained the organs of action—speech, hands, and so forth—remains while mentally recollecting sense objects under the pretext of meditation, is one of false conduct, a hypocrite. //6//
Baladeva: Now, if someone is seen who is devoid of the activity of passion and whose ears and other senses are sealed, regarding that case he says "the organs of action.

That ascetic who, having restrained the organs of action such as speech and so forth, remains under the pretext of meditation while recollecting the objects of the senses—sound, touch, and so on—is called one of deluded soul, a fool, and a hypocrite.

And for that ignorant person whose passion and other afflictions have been suppressed, because mental purity has not arisen through the performance of desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma*), even though there is no outward expansion of the ears and other senses, the mind remains impure; thus, due to the recollection of those objects by the mind, even one who strives for knowledge fails to attain it. Therefore, his practice is false, meaning he is a hypocrite whose observance of rules regarding speech and so forth is in vain. //6//
But he who, O Arjuna, restraining the senses with the mind, undertakes the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is preeminent. (3.7)

Śrīdhara: On the contrary, he says "But he who... to show that the performer of action who acts in this opposite manner is superior. "But he who, having restrained the senses with the mind and made them intent on the Lord, undertakes—that is, practices—the yoga consisting of action by means of the organs of action, being unattached, that is, free from desire for results."
He is distinguished; he becomes superior, meaning that through the purification of the mind he becomes possessed of knowledge. //7//

Madhusūdana: Out of mere eagerness, one should perform only desireless actions according to the scriptures for the purification of the mind, without renouncing all activities. Therefore, [the Lord says] "But he who... and so forth.
The word *tu* (but) serves to distinguish [this type of renunciant] from those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are impure.

Having restrained the senses—the organs of knowledge such as hearing and so forth—along with the mind, that is, having turned them away from attachment to objects such as sound which are causes of sin; or alternatively, having restrained them by means of a mind endowed with discrimination (*viveka*). With the organs of action, such as speech and hands, he undertakes—that is, performs—the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), which is prescribed as a cause of purification, being unattached, that is, devoid of desire for the fruits thereof. He who is thus discriminating is [distinguished] from the other.
It is superior to sexual misconduct;

for even when the exertion is equal, it becomes excellent by virtue of yielding a preeminent fruit. O Arjuna, behold this wonder: that one who restrains the organs of action while employing the organs of knowledge [is superior].
But the other, though devoid of the goals of human life, becomes a partaker of the supreme goal of man by restraining the organs of perception while employing the organs of action. //7//
Viśvanātha:
He says "But he who... to show that the householder who performs actions prescribed by the scriptures, being the opposite of this [latter], is superior;
"action-yoga" (karma-yoga) means that which is ordained by the scriptures.
"One who is unattached and free from desire for fruits is distinguished.
The venerable Śrī Rāmānujācārya explains that he is superior even to a person established in knowledge, by virtue of possessing a faith that is not based on worldly calculation. //7//
Baladeva: In contrast to this, he says "But he who... to show that even a householder who performs his own prescribed duties is superior.

He who, having restrained the senses—the ears and so forth—with a mind directed toward self-realization, being unattached—that is, free from desire for results—undertakes, or carries out, the yoga of action, which is the means consisting of ritual acts, he excels.
The meaning is that, because his knowledge is being cultivated, he becomes superior to the former. //7//
Perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction;
even the maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction.
Śrīdhara: "Niyatam" means:
since it is thus, therefore perform the obligatory (*niyata*) and constant (*nitya*) rites, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth;
for (*hi*) because...
The performance of action is superior—that is, more excellent—than the non-performance of all actions;
otherwise, for you who are free from action and devoid of all karma, even the maintenance of the body, the sustenance of the physical frame, would not be possible. (8)
Madhusūdana:

Since this is so, therefore, having restrained the organs of knowledge with the mind, you— though previously one who had not performed actions that cause purification— should perform the Vedic *niyata* (obligatory) action, which is prescribed by a specific injunction as being devoid of a connection to results, and which is performed for its own sake as a necessary duty.
Perform that which is known as the "daily Smārta rite.
By using the second-person imperative form "kuru" (perform), the word "tvam" (you) is already implied; thus, the explicit inclusion of the word "tvam" is shifted toward a different meaning.

Why? Because for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is impure, action alone must indeed be performed, since for one who does not act—that is, from the non-performance of action—action alone is superior (*jyāyas*), being more praiseworthy.
Not only would the purity of your internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) fail to be established in the absence of action,

but even the maintenance of your body— the physical subsistence of you who are inactive, being devoid of actions such as battle— would not be successfully accomplished in accordance with the characteristics of the Kṣatriya's duty.
And so it was stated previously.
Moreover, the word "api ca" (moreover) serves the purpose of adding [this] to the purification of the internal organ. //8//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, for you, the regular and constant performance of the twilight devotions (*sandhyopāsana*) and other rites is superior—that is, more excellent—than the state of non-action, which is the renunciation of all ritual acts (*karmasaṃnyāsa*).
For one who has renounced all actions, even the maintenance of the body would not be accomplished. //8//

Baladeva: "Niyatam" (necessarily). Therefore, you, whose mind is not yet purified, must necessarily perform that which is obligatory. The meaning is: for the sake of purifying the mind, perform your own prescribed duty without desire for results (*niṣkāmatayā*).

Action alone is superior—that is, more praiseworthy—than the renunciation of all action based merely on a restless longing for inaction, because it produces knowledge through the logic of ascending steps.
For knowledge does not arise in a defiled heart from one who abandons action out of mere restlessness.
Furthermore, for you who are inactive and have renounced all actions, even the maintenance of the body—the sustenance of the physical frame—would not be accomplished;
for as long as the completion of one's spiritual means requires it, the knower must perform actions such as wandering for alms in order to sustain that body.
And that is inappropriate for you, a Kṣatriya.

Therefore, having acquired wealth through the duties prescribed for you—such as warfare and the protection of subjects—and having ensured the maintenance of your body with those means, you should contemplate your own Self. //8//
Other than for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment. (3.9)

Śrīdhara: The Sāṅkhyas, however, say that since all action binds, nothing at all should be performed. Refuting that view, he says "yajñārthāt" (for the sake of sacrifice). Here, "sacrifice" refers to Viṣṇu.
According to the Vedic revelation, "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice"; therefore,
apart from action performed for the purpose of worshipping Him,
this world is bound by action— it is fettered by its own deeds.
But not for the sake of ritual action performed as a means of propitiating Īśvara.
Therefore, for that purpose—for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu—perform action properly, being free from attachment and devoid of desire. 9.
Madhusūdana: Thinking that,

according to the Smṛti— "A living being is bound by action" (Mbh 12.241.7)— all action, because it is of the nature of bondage, should not be performed by one who desires liberation, he states the following reply, beginning with "yajñārthāt."

The sacrifice is the Supreme Lord, for the Śruti declares, "Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu" (TaittS 1.7.4). Whatever action is performed for the sake of propitiating Him is for the sake of sacrifice; therefore, this world—consisting of those entitled to ritual action—is engaged in action other than that [sacrifice], and is bound by action, but not by that which is for the purpose of propitiating the Lord.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, for that purpose—for the sake of sacrifice—perform action;
being free from attachment and authorized for action, perform it properly, preceded by right faith and other such qualities. //9//
Viśvanātha:
[Objection: But then, since the Smṛti states, "A living being is bound by action," would there not be bondage when an action is performed? [Reply: No.
He states that action offered to the Supreme Lord is not binding by saying "yajñārthāt" (for the sake of sacrifice).

Sacrifice (*yajña*) is defined as dharma performed without desire and dedicated to Viṣṇu. Apart from that for which such action is intended, this world is bound by action; that is, one becomes fettered by action.
Therefore, for that purpose—for the sake of accomplishing such dharma—you should perform action.

Now, one might object: "Even dharma dedicated to Viṣṇu becomes a cause of bondage if it is performed with desires in view. To this He says: "Free from attachment," meaning devoid of longing for results.
In this very same way, the Blessed Lord spoke to Uddhava:
O Uddhava, one who remains established in his own duty, performing sacrifices without desire for rewards,
goes neither to heaven nor to hell.
Provided that he does not perform anything else.
Abiding in this world, established in his own duty, sinless and pure,
he attains purified knowledge.
"Or devotion to Me by chance. (BhP 11.20.10–1) //9//

Baladeva: [Objection: Surely bondage would arise when action is performed, because of such traditional teachings as, "A living being is bound by action," and so forth. To this, he says: "For the sake of sacrifice" (*yajñārthāt*).
Sacrifice is the Supreme Lord, according to the Vedic revelation: "Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu."

If one performs action other than that which has the fruit of pleasing Him—that is, action whose fruit is one's own pleasure—this world of living beings becomes bound by karma; they are fettered by their actions.
Therefore, perform action for His sake, for the purpose of pleasing Viṣṇu.

O Kaunteya, being free from attachment and having abandoned the desire for personal pleasure, one is not bound when, having worshipped Viṣṇu with sacrifices and other rites accomplished through wealth acquired by righteous means, one maintains the journey of the body with what remains from those offerings.
This is the meaning. //9//
In the beginning, Prajāpati, having created living beings together with sacrifice, said: "By this shall you multiply; let this be the cow of plenty that grants your desired objects. (3.10)
Śrīdhara: Even based on the words of Prajāpati, he states that the performer of action alone is superior with the words "sahayajñāḥ" (those accompanied by sacrifice).

Those who exist together with sacrifice are "sahayajñāḥ"—the subjects, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, who are entitled to perform sacrifice. Having created them at the beginning of creation, Brahmā said this: "By means of this sacrifice, you shall procreate. For "procreation" (prasava) indeed means growth.
The meaning is: "May you attain ever-increasing prosperity.
The reason for this is:
"This sacrifice of yours is a cow that milks all desired objects."
"He milks what is desired" means likewise;
the sense is that he may be the bestower of desired enjoyments.
And here, the mention of "sacrifice" (yajña) is for the purpose of indicating necessary duties (āvaśyaka-karma).

As for the praise of optional ritual action (*kāmya-karma*), although it is not directly relevant to the present context, there is no fault, as it serves the general purpose of showing that action is superior to non-action. //10//
Madhusūdana says that even according to the word of Prajāpati, one who is authorized must perform action; he states this in four verses beginning with "sahayajñā.
Those who exist "with sacrifice"—that is, together with the collection of prescribed actions—are called "sahayajñā," meaning those who are properly authorized.
In the alternative view where the rule *vopasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.82) applies, there is an absence of the substitution of *sa*.
Having created the three classes of beings (*prajāḥ*) at the beginning of the previous aeon, the Lord of Creatures, the Creator, spoke.
To the question "What did he say?", he replies: "By means of this sacrifice—the dharma appropriate to your respective stages of life (*āśrama*)—you shall procreate; you shall bring forth offspring."
*Prasava* means growth;
the sense is: "May you obtain ever-increasing prosperity.
To explain how growth may be attained through this, he says: "This dharma called sacrifice is the cow that milks your desired objects for you."
It is so called because it milks—that is, it bestows or causes one to attain—desired and cherished objects of desire, which are the fruits of action;
the meaning is that it grants the enjoyment of what is wished for.
Here, although the mention of "sacrifice" (yajña) is intended as an illustration of obligatory duties, since the sin incurred by their non-performance will be explained later.

Furthermore, there is no occasion for the discussion of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) in this context, because they have already been rejected by the statement, "Let me not be the cause of the fruit of action.
Likewise, since obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) possess incidental fruits (*ānuṣaṅgika-phala*), it is appropriate [to say],
"May this be the milch-cow of your desired objects."

And so Āpastamba records in his Smṛti: "Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary effects, even so when dharma is practiced, worldly benefits arise as secondary effects; if they do not arise, there is no loss of dharma.
Even though the fruit exists, the distinction between optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) rites lies in the presence or absence of the intention for that fruit.
Even in the case of that which is not intentionally produced, there is no distinction in its arising from the intrinsic nature of the thing itself;
this will be demonstrated in detail further on. //10//
Viśvanātha:
It has been stated that for one whose mind is impure, one should perform only desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma*) and not renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

Now, he says in these seven verses beginning with "saha" that if one is unable even to become desireless, then one should perform even duty with desire, dedicating it to Viṣṇu, but one must not abandon action.
In the compound *sahayajñāḥ*, the form *sahayajñāḥ* (rather than *sayajñāḥ*) occurs because the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* is not applied here according to the rule *vopasarjanasya*.

Having created subjects who performed dharma dedicated to Viṣṇu from of old, Brahmā said: "By this dharma you shall propagate yourselves"—the meaning is that *prasavaḥ* (propagation) signifies growth, that you may attain ever-increasing prosperity.
Observing their state of possessing desire, He said: "May this sacrifice be for you a cow that milks all desires—that which grants whatever is wished for. This is the meaning. //10//
Baladeva says: He states the fault for one who maintains the journey of the body with what remains from that which is not the residue of sacrifice.

Prajāpati is Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, according to such Vedic texts as "the Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self," and according to such Smṛti passages as "He is Acyuta, the Brahmā and the Lord of creatures."

The meaning is as follows: in the beginning of creation, having first created beings in the form of gods, humans, and so forth—along with sacrifices, that is, accompanied by sacrifices—who were devoid of the differentiation of names and forms, merged within Himself whose power is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and were thus unfit for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*); He then ordained them to possess names and forms that would accomplish those goals, and manifested sacrifice and the Veda which defines it.
To them, the Compassionate One said this:
"By means of this sacrifice declared in the Veda and offered to Me, you shall multiply;
'prasava' means growth—therefore, the sense is: may you attain your own increase."

May this sacrifice, offered by me to you, fulfill your desired wishes; through the purification of the heart, the realization of self-knowledge, and the accomplishment of the maintenance of the body, may it grant the liberation you seek. 10.
Sustain the gods with this [offering], and let those gods sustain you. Sustaining one another, you shall attain the supreme good. 11.
Śrīdhara: How can sacrifice be the milker of desired objects?
To this he says: "The gods.
Sustain the gods by means of this sacrifice.
"May you cause the oblations to increase through their respective portions, and may those gods cause you to increase by means of rain and so forth, through the production of food.
Thus, increasing one another—both you and the gods—you shall repeatedly attain and reach mutual prosperity. (11)
Madhusūdana:
As for how the sacrifice is the "milk-cow of desired objects," he says, "the gods.
By this sacrifice, you who are the sacrificers should nourish—the meaning is, you should cause to grow and satisfy—the gods, Indra and the others, with the enjoyment of the oblations.
Those gods, having been cultivated by you, shall cultivate you in turn; that is, they shall cause you to flourish by means of the production of food through rain and other such benefits.

Thus, mutually supporting one another, both the gods and yourselves shall attain the desired goal—the excellent and superior welfare. The meaning is that the gods will attain satisfaction, and you shall attain the supreme excellence known as heaven. //11//
Viśvanātha: [To the question] "How can sacrifice be the bestower of desired objects?", he says: "The gods...
By means of this sacrifice, cause the gods to prosper.
"Be full of being (bhāva).
"Being" means affection; the meaning is: act so as to be endowed with that [affection], that is, gladden [them].
May those gods also gladden you. //11//
Baladeva said: "And you, O subjects, being engaged in this sacrifice, nourish the gods—who have become my own limbs—by offering them their respective oblations, and thus make them pleased.

May those gods, being pleased, nourish you by granting their boons. In this way, nourishing one another with pure food, you shall attain the supreme good characterized by liberation; for purity of food is indeed a limb of steadfastness in knowledge."

In this regard, according to the Vedic scripture: "When there is purity of food, there is purity of the inner being (sattva); when there is purity of the inner being, there is steady mindfulness; and when mindfulness is attained, there is liberation from all knots. //11//
For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will bestow upon you the enjoyments you desire.
He who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is indeed a thief. 12.
Śrīdhara, clarifying this very point, states the fault in the non-performance of action: "iṣṭān" and so forth.
The gods, being nourished by sacrifices, will indeed bestow enjoyments upon you through the medium of rain and other such means.
Therefore, he who eats the food and other things given by the gods without first offering them to these very gods through the five great sacrifices and other rites—[incurs a fault].
He should be known as a thief and indeed a robber. //12//
Madhusūdana:
[The Lord] says "desired" (iṣṭān) to show that the fruit of sacrifice is not only pertaining to the next world, but also to this world.
The gods will grant—that is, bestow—upon you the desired enjoyments, such as cattle, food, gold, and so forth;

for they have been nourished and satisfied by sacrifices. Since those enjoyments have been given to you by them as if it were a debt, [you should give] those enjoyments given by the gods back to them.

He who eats without first giving to the gods—that is, without performing the oblations in the sacrifices dedicated to the gods—satisfies only his own body and senses; he is indeed a thief, a robber, for he is a stealer of the gods' property, since he has failed to discharge his debt to the gods.
Viśvanātha:
Clarifying this very point, he states the fault in the non-performance of one's duty with the words "iṣṭān" (desired).
The meaning is: "Do not withhold the food and other things bestowed by them through means such as rain."
He who eats without first giving to these deities through the five great sacrifices and other rites is indeed a thief. //12//
Baladeva, clarifying this very point, states the defect arising from the performance of ritual action with the words "iṣṭān" (desired).

The meaning is: the gods, who have previously been cultivated as your own limbs, will grant you—O seekers of liberation—the desired enjoyments that are longed for and depend upon successive sacrifices; that is to say, by means of rain and so forth, they will produce rice and other grains.

He who eats for his own gratification alone, without offering those enjoyments—which were given by the gods for the sake of their own worship—through the five great sacrifices and other rites, is indeed a thief and a robber.
Since the gods take those offerings away from him to nourish themselves, he deserves punishment from Yama, like a thief from a king; such a person is unworthy of the goals of human life. (12)
The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins; but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake alone eat only sin. (3.13)
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "those who eat the remnants of sacrifice" (yajña-śiṣṭāśinaḥ) to show that only those who sacrifice are superior, and not others.
Those who eat what remains from sacrifices such as the Vaiśvadeva are liberated from all sins committed through the five slaughter-houses.
And five slaughterhouses are mentioned in the Smṛti: the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom;
by these five slaughterhouses of the householder, one does not find heaven.
Those who cook solely for their own food, and not for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and other rites, are sinful and ill-behaved; they consume only evil. //13//
Madhusūdana:

But those who eat the nectar that remains from sacrifices such as the Vaiśvadeva— those virtuous ones being "cultured" (śiṣṭa) because they perform what is enjoined by the Vedas— they are liberated from all [debts] incurred by the non-performance of prescribed duties and from those previously committed, since they have discharged their debts to the gods and others.

And by means of the sins characterized by the five slaughterhouses, they become untouched by past or future transgressions; this is the meaning. Having thus stated the absence of past and future sins in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he states the fault in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): those who do not perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites consume only sin (*agha*).
The word *tu* is used for emphasis.

Those who, being sinful, cook solely for their own sake—having committed sins on account of the five slaughterhouses (*pañca-sūnā*) and on account of violence committed through negligence—and not for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites;

and thus, while the sin committed by the five slaughterhouses and so forth already exists, they incur another sin caused by the non-performance of the obligatory daily rites such as the *vaiśvadeva*—those sinners, indeed, consume their own evil.
It has been said; and likewise the Smṛti:
"The grinding-stone, the mortar, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom."
"A householder has five slaughterhouses; through them, he does not find heaven.
And: "The sin committed by the five slaughterhouses one removes by means of the five sacrifices.
And the Śruti says: "That which is eaten here is his common food for all [beings]."
"He who venerates this [world] does not turn away from evil, for this is mixed," so says the Vedic verse: "The one whose mind is set on the tip [of the blade] obtains food in vain."
I speak the truth: his death is indeed certain; he does not nourish his friend who does not honor him.
He who eats alone becomes one who eats alone for nothing. Thus it is said.
And this is an illustration [of the principle] regarding the five great sacrifices (pañca-mahā-yajña), both those prescribed by the Smṛtis and those prescribed by the Śruti;
the meaning of Prajāpati’s statement is that one who is qualified must necessarily perform these obligatory rites. //13//
Viśvanātha:

Those who eat food remaining from sacrifices such as the Vaiśvadeva are liberated from all sins committed through the five slaughter-houses (*pañca-sūnā*). These five slaughter-houses are described in the Smṛtis: [text continues].
"The mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom—these are the five slaughterhouses of the householder; through them, he does not find heaven. (13)

Baladeva: Those virtuous ones who, having worshipped Viṣṇu—the Lord of All—who abides as the sacrifice through His limbs such as Indra and others, and who subsist on the remnants of that worship to maintain their bodily existence, are devotees of the Lord of All, the Person of Sacrifice; they are liberated from all sins—every single transgression accumulated since beginningless time that obstructs the experience of the Self.

But those wicked ones, seized by evil, consume only sin; they cook for their own nourishment that which was given by the Sacrificial Person (yajña-puruṣa)—who exists as the limbs of various deities—for the purpose of His own worship, namely rice and other grains. The meaning is that they bring about their own nourishment by cooking it. It is called "sin" because the cooked rice and other grains undergo a transformation into the form of sin. //13//
From food all beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food; from sacrifice rain comes into being; and sacrifice originates from action. (14)
Śrīdhara: He states with three verses beginning with "From food" that action must be performed because it is the cause for the continued functioning of the cycle of the world.
From food, transformed into the form of semen and blood, living beings are produced;
and the origin of food is from *parjanya*, which is rain.
And that rain-cloud arises from sacrifice;
and that sacrifice originates from action—
meaning it is properly accomplished through action, such as the ritual activities of the sacrificer and others.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. 14.
Madhusūdana:

Not only must action be performed because of the word of Prajāpati, but also because it is the cause for the continued functioning of the wheel of the world; thus he says with three verses beginning with "From food.
From food that has been eaten, having been transformed into the form of semen and blood, living beings—the bodies of sentient creatures—come into being, that is, they are born.
The "origination from food" (*anna-sambhava*) refers to the birth [of beings] from food;
this is indeed established by direct perception.

Regarding this, he states the application of ritual action (*karman*): Parjanya arises from sacrifice (*yajña*), such as the *Kārīrī* and the *Agnihotra*, through the merit (*dharma*) known as the *apūrva*.
And how the oblation of the Agnihotra produces rain has been explained in the Aṣṭādhyāyī-kāṇḍa, in the form of the "Six Questions" dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya.
And it was stated by Manu:
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun."
"From the sun rain is born; from rain, food; and from that, living beings" (Manu 3.76).
And that sacrifice, known as Dharma, is subtle, originates from action, and is accomplished through the activities of the officiating priests and the patron.
For prescribed action is the cause of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the sacrifice. //14//
Viśvanātha:

He states that one must indeed perform sacrifice because it is the cause for the continued functioning of the wheel of the world. From food, living beings—meaning sentient creatures—come into existence; thus, food is the cause of living beings.
Since the bodies of living beings are established only from that very food when it has been transformed into the form of semen and blood, Parjanya (the rain-god) is the cause of that food.
Since food is produced by rains alone, the sacrifice is the cause of that rain;

since the appropriate clouds that bestow rain are produced only by the sacrifice performed by people, the sacrifice is the cause of that [rain]. Because the sacrifice is accomplished through action—which consists of the activities of the officiating priests and the patron—the sacrifice is established through action alone.

Baladeva says: "From food" [refers to this]; having created living beings through Prajāpati, the Supreme Lord, He simultaneously created the sacrifice for their sustenance. Therefore, one who follows the Supreme Lord must necessarily perform it; thus he says, "from food."
Living beings—that is, sentient creatures—come into existence from food such as rice and other grains;
for it is through that food, transformed into the form of semen and blood, that their bodies are produced.
The production of that food, in turn, comes from Parjanya, which is to say, from rain.
And from sacrifice comes Parjanya; the meaning is that it is accomplished.
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain food, and from that, living beings."
Thus, according to the *Manusmṛti*. //14//
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable (Akṣara). Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice. //15//
Śrīdhara: "And likewise, know that action" means:
know that action, which consists of the activities of the sacrificer and others, as originating from Brahman;
*brahman* here refers to the Veda.
Therefore, know that [the Veda] has proceeded from Him;
for the Śruti says: "This Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvāṅgirasa are the breath of this Great Being."
Since the sacrifice is so highly intended as proceeding from the Imperishable (akṣara) itself,
therefore the all-pervading Brahman, though eternal, is always established in sacrifice;
it is said to be "established in sacrifice" because it is attained through sacrifice, which serves as the means.
It is as in the saying, "Fortune always dwells with the industrious.

Alternatively, since action is the root of the wheel of the world, the Brahman known as the Veda— though it is omnipresent, being established in all [texts] such as the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of the mantras and the accounts of actual events (*bhūtārthākhyāna*) which convey accomplished facts— is nevertheless always firmly established in the sacrifice by way of its primary purport (*tātparya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that ritual actions such as sacrifice must be performed. //15//
Madhusūdana:
And that [knowledge] produces what was previously non-existent.
"Born of Brahman" means that the Veda is Brahman; it is that which has the Veda as its source and authority. Thus it is said.
Know that only the action prescribed by the Veda is the means for accomplishing the *apūrva*, and not anything else propounded by heretics; this is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: what is the distinction of the Veda compared to the scriptures of heretics, such that dharma is established solely by the Veda?

To the objection that it is not something else, he says: "Brahman, known as the Veda, which has its origin in the Imperishable. That which has its origin—its manifestation—from the Imperishable (akṣara), the faultless Supreme Self (paramātman), by way of being the breath of the Person (puruṣa-niḥśvāsa-nyāyena) and not through prior intellectual deliberation, is "originating from the Imperishable. Thus, the sense is that the Vedic statement, being non-human in origin, has all suspicion of defect removed and is the producer of valid knowledge (pramiti).

And thus says the Śruti: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, as well as the Atharva-Aṅgirasa, history (itihāsa), ancient lore (purāṇa), sciences (vidyā), secret doctrines (upaniṣads), verses (śloka), aphorisms (sūtra), expositions (anuvyākhyāna), and commentaries (vyākhyāna)— these are the breathings of this Great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10).

Therefore, because it arises directly from the Supreme Self, the Veda—known as Brahman—is omnipresent, illuminating all things, eternal, and indestructible; it is established with full intent in sacrifice, which is known as Dharma and transcends the senses. Thus, the meaning is that one must abandon the pseudo-dharmas propounded by heretics and practice only that Dharma revealed by the Veda. //15//
Viśvanātha:
The cause of that action is Brahman, which is the Veda;
for it is precisely from hearing the injunctive statements declared in the Veda that the activity toward sacrifice arises. Therefore, the cause of that Veda is the Imperishable Brahman.
For the Vedas originate from Brahman alone; and thus says the Śruti: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvāṅgirasas are the breath of this Great Being."
Therefore, the meaning is that since Brahman is all-pervading and established in sacrifice, Brahman is also attained through sacrifice.

Although here the categories of things, beginning with food and ending with Brahman, have been described in terms of the relationship between cause and effect, nevertheless, among those very things, it is sacrifice that is enjoined by the scripture;
thus, it alone is the subject under discussion.
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings"—so says the Smṛti. (15)
Baladeva: Know that this [action], consisting of the activities of the officiating priests and others, originates from Brahman;
the meaning is that you should understand its commencement from the Veda (Brahman).
And know that this Brahman, in the form of the Veda, is manifestly originated from the Imperishable Supreme Lord.
This is because of such scriptural declarations as: "This *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, [and] the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ* are the breath of this Great Being.

Since sacrifice is so dear to Him—being the means of subsistence for the creatures He Himself has created—therefore, although Brahman is omnipresent and all-pervading, it is eternally and at all times established in sacrifice; by that very fact, it is [sustained].
The meaning is "it is attained. //15//
He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion here in this world— he, O Pārtha, lives in vain, for he is of sinful life and delights in the senses.

Śrīdhara: Since the wheel of action and so forth has been set in motion by the Supreme Lord himself for the sake of accomplishing the human goals of living beings, therefore the life of one who does not perform that [action] is in vain;
thus he says, "In this way.
From the Veda—known as Brahman—which consists of the words of the Supreme Lord, there arises the engagement of persons in action.
From that comes the accomplishment of action;
from that, the rain-cloud;
from that, food.
From that arise the primary elements;
from the primary elements, the activity of karma proceeds in the same manner.
He who does not turn nor follow this wheel thus set in motion is one whose life is wretched.
He is one whose life is "agha," meaning of the nature of evil,
because he delights only in sense objects through his senses, and not in action performed for the sake of propitiating the Lord.
Therefore, he lives in vain and for no purpose. //16//
Madhusūdana: It is indeed so; what follows from that? He says "evam" (thus):
