from the Supreme Lord comes the manifestation of the Vedas, which illuminate everything and are eternal and faultless.
From that comes the full understanding of action; from that, through its performance, arises dharma;
from that, the rain-cloud; from that, food; from that, living beings; and again, in the same manner, the activity of living beings proceeds.
Thus, he who does not follow nor perform this wheel set in motion by the Supreme Lord, which sustains the entire world—[he is lost].

Such a person, whose life is sinful and whose livelihood is wicked, lives in vain and for no purpose, O Pārtha; for him, death is better than life, because in another birth there is the possibility of practicing dharma—this is the meaning.
And thus says the Śruti: "Now, this self is indeed the world of all beings; whatever one offers as an oblation, whatever one sacrifices..."

"By that [offering], he gains the world of the gods; then, by what he recites, he gains the world of the seers; then, by what he offers to the ancestors, and by what he desires offspring, he gains the world of the ancestors; then, by what he shelters men and gives them food, he gains the world of men; then, by what he provides grass and water for animals, he gains the world of animals; and by what dogs, birds, and even ants subsist in his house, he gains the world of those. [BAU 1.4.16]
The phrase "one who delights in the senses" (indriyārāmaḥ) excludes the knower of Brahman (brahmavid).

Since he delights in sense objects by means of the senses, he is entitled to ritual action; therefore, the intention is that by not performing such actions, he merely accumulates sin and lives in vain. //16//
Viśvanātha:
He states the transgression incurred by failing to perform this [practice] with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
The wheel is set in motion by means of its front and rear portions.
From sacrifice comes rain;
from rain, food;
from food, man.
From the person comes the sacrifice,
and from the sacrifice comes Parjanya; he who does not turn this cycle around by performing the sacrifice— that is, does not cause it to revolve—
is one whose life is possessed by evil (aghāyuḥ).
The sense is: who would not sink into hell? //16//
Baladeva: With the words "Thus," he states the fault in not performing sacrifice.
From the Supreme Brahman comes the manifestation of the Vedas; from that, the awakening of Brahman, [arises] sacrifice; from that, Parjanya (the rain-god);
from that, food; from that, living beings; and again, in the same manner, the engagement of living beings in action—thus [sacrifice] is the sustainer of the entire universe.
That person who does not follow the wheel set in motion by the Supreme Lord, the Prajāpati, is turned away from the Supreme Lord;
living a life of sin, he lives in vain and fruitlessly.
O Pārtha, this is because he delights only in sense-objects through his senses, and not in sacrifice—which is intended for the Supreme Brahman—nor in eating the remnants of that sacrifice. (16)
But for that man who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be performed. (3.17)

Śrīdhara: Thus, having described the yoga of action for the sake of purifying the internal organ of the ignorant person through the passage beginning with "Not by the undertaking of actions," he declares the uselessness of action for the knower in two verses beginning with "But he who...
He is one whose delight—that is, love—is in the Self alone.

Therefore, one who is satisfied in the Self alone, contented through the experience of his own bliss, and for that very reason gratified in the Self alone, being devoid of expectation for objects of enjoyment—for such a person there is no duty to perform. //17//
Madhusūdana:

He who does not delight in the objects of the senses but perceives the supreme reality, even though he performs actions that serve as the cause for the wheel of the world and so forth, does not incur sin because his purpose has been fulfilled;
thus [the Lord] says in two verses beginning with "yas tu."

For one who delights in the senses experiences pleasure (*rati*) in garlands, sandalwood, women, and the like; satisfaction (*tṛpti*) in agreeable food, drink, and so forth; and contentment (*tuṣṭi*) through the acquisition of cattle, sons, gold, and the like, as well as by the absence of disease and other ailments.

Since the absence of pleasure, dissatisfaction, lack of satisfaction, and discontent is observed among those possessed of passion when the aforementioned objects are unavailable, it follows that pleasure, satisfaction, and contentment are specific modifications of the mind established by direct experience (*sākṣi-siddha*).

However, one whose mind has attained the Supreme Self does not desire the happiness of sense-objects because of the absence of the perception of duality and because such happiness is exceedingly trivial; this was stated in the passage beginning, "As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir... (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7.18.1).

Therefore, because there is an absence of delight, satisfaction, and contentment directed toward objects that are not the Self, one who directly realizes the Self as supreme bliss and non-dual is described metaphorically in this way: "delighting in the Self, satisfied with the Self, and contented with the Self.
And so says the Śruti: "sporting in the Self..."
"One who finds delight in the Self, who is active [in yoga], is indeed the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "one who is satisfied in the Self" (*ātmatṛptaś ca*) serves to draw back the force of the word "indeed" (*eva*).

By using the term "human being" (*mānava*), it is intended to convey that anyone at all who is such as this has accomplished his purpose, and not merely by excellence of caste, such as being a Brāhmaṇa.
And in the phrase "satisfied in the Self alone," the word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction.
For one who is thus [situated], because of the absence of any cause for qualification, there exists no ritual duty whatsoever, whether Vedic or worldly. //17//
Viśvanātha:

Thus it has been stated that even one who possesses desire should perform action when there is a lack of capacity due to being free from desire. However, he who has ascended to the stage of knowledge because of the purity of his inner organ never performs either obligatory or optional rites; this he states in the following two verses beginning with "yas tu."

Delighting in the self, rejoicing in the self, because he is satisfied with the self, he is contented through the experience of bliss in the self. Let him not be contented within himself alone, nor even find some small satisfaction in the enjoyment of external objects;
rather, he says "not at all" in this regard. In the self alone—and not in the enjoyment of external objects—there is no work for him to be done as a duty. //17//

Baladeva: Regarding the one who has beheld the Self through the knowledge that constitutes His very nature—which has arisen upon the mirror of the mind being polished by desireless action and by the worship of Me—as stated by Me, He says in two verses beginning with "But he who... that for such a person there is no further duty to perform.
He is one for whom there is delight in the Self, his own essential nature, which is characterized by the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin;
he is satisfied by the Self, which is self-luminous bliss when perceived, and not by food, drink, and the like;
and he is contented in such a Self alone, and not in dancing, singing, and so forth.
For one who is thus constituted, there exists no action whatsoever to be performed for the sake of beholding that [reality], because its own essential nature is eternally perceived. //17//
For him there is no purpose whatsoever served by action performed here, nor any by action left undone;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire.

Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this with the words "not at all. There is no merit (puṇya) whatsoever for him through performed action (kṛtena karmaṇā), nor is there any transgression (pratyavāya) whatsoever through non-performance (akṛtena).
Because one who is free from egoism transcends both injunctions and prohibitions;
nevertheless, as the Śruti states, "Therefore, that which humans know is not dear to these gods," there may be obstacles created by the gods regarding liberation.
Anticipating this, it is said that for the sake of avoiding such obstacles, the gods should be served through ritual actions.
Among all beings, from Brahmā down to the immovable, there is no "resort for any purpose"— the word *vyapāśraya* here means simply a resort.
The meaning is that he has no purpose (*artha*) to be resorted to, namely liberation (*mokṣa*),
because the absence of obstacles has already been stated by the scripture itself.
And so says the Śruti: "Neither the gods nor non-existence can prevail over him; for he becomes their very Self"—so it is heard.
The indeclinable *ha* has the sense of *api* (even).

The meaning of the Śruti is that even the gods are not able (*neśate*), that is, they have no power, to bring about his non-existence (*abhūtyai*), which is to say, to obstruct his attainment of the state of Brahman, for he has become the Self of them.

But obstacles created by the gods occur only prior to the arising of perfect knowledge; for by stating that "what this Brahman is which men know is not dear to these gods," the fact that the gods act as obstructors is indicated precisely in relation to that knowledge of Brahman—
thus says Madhusūdana.

Now, one might object that even for the knower of the Self, there may be action for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), for the sake of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), or for the sake of avoiding transgression; therefore, he says "not at all" (*naiva*).

For him who delights in the Self, there is no purpose or motive—characterized either as worldly prosperity or the highest good—to be achieved by performed action, because he has no desire for prosperity such as heaven and the like, and because the highest good cannot be accomplished through action.
And so says the Śruti: "Having examined the worlds acquired through action, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment, [realizing] that 'there is nothing uncreated [attained] by means of what is created'.
The meaning is that liberation, which is uncreated and eternal, does not exist through created action.
By the use of the particle *eva*, the exclusion of even that which is to be accomplished through knowledge is indicated.
For the supreme good, which is of the nature of the Self, is eternally attained; its non-attainment is due solely to ignorance.
And that [non-attainment] is to be removed by the mere knowledge of reality.

The meaning is that when that [ignorance] has been dispelled by the knowledge of reality, for that knower of the Self, there remains no purpose whatsoever to be accomplished through action or to be accomplished through knowledge.
Even for one who has become such [a knower], ritual actions must indeed be performed for the sake of avoiding transgression; therefore, he says: "Not by non-performance.
This is a past passive participle used in the sense of existence (*bhāve*).
By the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), there is no purpose whatsoever attained in this world, whether in the form of being censured or in the form of incurring transgression.
He states the reason for this in the second half of the verse.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Because for this knower of the Self, there exists no dependence on any purpose or connection to any objective among all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects.
The meaning of the sentence is that there is no object to be accomplished by action depending upon any particular element (bhūta-viśeṣa).

Therefore, for him, what has been done and what has not been done is purposeless; as the Śruti says: "Neither what has been done nor what has not been done afflicts him. And from the Śruti: "Even the gods have no power over his non-existence, for he becomes their very Self," even the gods [have no power] over him.

The intention is that, because it has been stated that [rites] are not capable of producing liberation, the performance of ritual action in the form of worshipping the gods is not even for the sake of removing obstacles.
Such a state of the knower of Brahman has been described by Vasiṣṭha through the division of the seven stages:
"The first stage of knowledge is proclaimed as being called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious)."
The second is vicāraṇā, and the third is tanu-mānasā.

"The fourth would be the descent into existence (*sattvāpatti*); after that, the nose-less (*asaṃsaktināsikā*); the sixth is the non-contemplation of objects (*padārthābhāvanī*); and the seventh is known as the one that has gone beyond the fourth (*turyagā*).
In this context, the first is the desire for liberation, preceded by the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities and culminating in its fruit.
Then, having approached a guru, the investigation of the Vedānta texts consisting of hearing and reflection constitutes the second stage.
Then, through the practice of meditative absorption (nididhyāsana), the mind’s capacity to grasp subtle objects by means of one-pointedness constitutes the third stage.
These three stages, which take the form of spiritual means, are called the waking state (jāgrad-avasthā) by yogis.
Because the world appears with differentiation, it has been said:
"O Rāma, this triad of stages is established as the waking state;
for in the waking state, this world is perceived through the cognition of differentiation according to its true nature."

Then, from the Vedānta statements, the non-conceptual direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the identity of Brahman and the Self—the fourth stage, which is the fruit-form attainment of being (*sattvāpatti*)—is called the dream state; for everything in the world manifests as illusory. As it has been said: "When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest..."
"Those who have reached the fourth stage perceive the world as if in a dream.
Thus, this yogi who has attained the fourth stage is called a "knower of Brahman" (brahmavit).
However, the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are merely internal subdivisions of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

In that state, when the mind has been restrained through the practice of conceptual samādhi, that state of non-conceptual samādhi is called "non-attachment" (asaṃsakti) and also "deep sleep" (suṣupti),
because from it one awakens by oneself alone.
Such a yogi is the most excellent knower of Brahman.
Then, through the maturation of that practice, it becomes a long-lasting contemplation of the non-existence of objects; this is called "deep sleep" (*gāḍha-suṣupti*).
Because the yogin who has thus practiced by himself emerges from that state only through the effort of another, he is the most excellent knower of Brahman (*brahmavid varīyān*). For it has been said:
"Having reached the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep,
one gradually falls into the sixth stage, called profound deep sleep"— thus it is said.
In this state of samādhi, however, one does not emerge either by oneself or through another, because there is an absolute absence of the perception of duality.

However, always being absorbed in that [state] alone, even without his own effort, with his bodily functions carried out by others through the power of the vital breath impelled by the Supreme Lord, he remains everywhere as a mass of perfect supreme bliss;
that is the seventh state, the fourth (turiya).
Having attained that, he is called the most excellent knower of Brahman. For it has been said:
"Abiding on the sixth stage, he shall attain the seventh stage;
he is either somewhat perfected, or else he is nothing at all."
"However, liberation while in the body (videha-muktatā) is said to be the seventh stage of yoga;
it is beyond the reach of words, peaceful, and the ultimate limit among the stages of yoga.
With reference to this, it is recorded in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:
The perfected one does not perceive the body— whether it be decaying, stationary, or arisen— since he has realized his own true nature;
whether it has departed due to fate or arrived through the power of fate.
Like one blinded by the intoxication of wine who has dressed himself in fine garments.
Even the body, subject to destiny, remains alive as long as it observes its own originating karma;
yet one who has ascended to the yoga of samādhi transcends that body along with its manifold phenomenal world.
Furthermore, one who has awakened to reality no longer experiences the dream state.

And the Śruti says: "Just as a snake that has cast off its skin lies dead and discarded in an anthill, even so does this body lie; but this bodiless, immortal life-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed Brahman, it is indeed light.
Herein is the summary:
The fourth stage is knowledge; the first three are said to be the means.
The latter three are proclaimed as the states of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

The intention here is that even an ignorant person who has ascended to the first three stages has no authority regarding ritual action, let alone one who possesses knowledge of reality or one who is liberated while living, who is distinguished by that knowledge. //18//
Viśvanātha:
There is no purpose nor any fruit from a deed performed;
nor is there any harm whatsoever from one not performed.

Because for him, among all beings—from the stationary entities within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) upwards—there is no one whatsoever who must be relied upon or sought as a refuge for the sake of any purpose or for his own benefit.
In the Purāṇas and other texts, the word "vyapāśraya" is used in this very sense, as in: "For men who carry devotion toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva... [and so forth].
"In this world, there is no support whatsoever for knowledge, dispassion, and vigor" (BhP 6.17.31);
likewise, "those who take refuge in that refuge are purified" (BhP 2.7.46).
In such passages as "the refuge is the cause of the state," the prefix *apa-* is seen to have no additional meaning. //18//
Baladeva: There is no purpose or fruit whatsoever in performing actions for the sake of attaining that vision;
nor is there any harm, characterized by the loss of that vision, incurred here by not performing such actions, because [the vision] consists of the natural perception of the Self.
Even one such as this, though fearing obstacles created by the gods, would not perform action consisting of their worship for the sake of pleasing them;
for the Śruti declares that the gods are enemies of knowledge: "Therefore, that which humans know is not dear to these gods. To this, he says: "Not so," and so forth.

For this wise man who has attained self-realization, among all beings— whether gods or humans— there is no one whatsoever who, for the sake of some purpose, must be relied upon as a refuge through ritual actions to ensure freedom from obstacles.
Since obstacles created by the gods arise only prior to the dawning of knowledge, once self-delight is established, those obstacles caused by them cannot occur due to its power.
For it is heard in scripture: "Neither the gods nor non-existence have power over him, for he becomes their very self.
The particle *ha* is used here in the sense of *api* (even).
Thus, even the gods [have no power] over that one who experiences the Self.
They are not capable of attaining prosperity or the destruction of their own suffering, because that Self is as dear to them as it is to Him; such is the meaning. //18//
Therefore, perform always the duty that must be done without attachment; for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme. 19.

Śrīdhara: Since it is only for such a knower that action has no utility, and not for anyone else, He says "Therefore" [in verse 19] to tell him, "Perform action. Being unattached—meaning free from attachment to results—one should perform properly the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) actions prescribed as necessary duties.
For, by performing action without attachment, a person attains the supreme liberation through the gateway of mental purification and knowledge. //19//
Madhusūdana:
Since you are not such a knower (*jñānī*), but rather a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who is merely entitled to ritual action (*karmādhikṛta*),

you must always— that is, at all times, and not only occasionally— perform that which is necessary to be done (*avaśya-kartavya*), remaining unattached, meaning free from desire for the fruits [of action].

Perform properly and accomplish according to the scriptures that very action— characterized as obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika)— which is enjoined by the Vedic revelation beginning with "as long as life lasts" and which is applied to knowledge by the scripture stating, "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting."

For since a person who acts without attachment, performing action for the sake of the Lord, attains supreme liberation by means of the purification of the mind and the attainment of knowledge—he alone is a true person (sat-puruṣa), and no other; such is the intended meaning. //19//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, you lack the fitness for ascending the stages of knowledge; furthermore, as one possessed of true discrimination, you have no entitlement whatsoever to rites performed for the sake of desired rewards.
Therefore, He says "tasmāt" (therefore), meaning: perform action indeed without desire for fruit;
"kāryam" refers to that which is enjoined as necessarily to be done, leading to the supreme liberation. //19//
Baladeva: Since for one who has attained the vision of the Self, ritual action is of no further use, therefore you should perform such action as is enjoined as a duty.

Doing so while being unattached—meaning free from the desire for results—you attain, that is, perceive in its true nature, the Supreme Self which is distinct from the body and other such limiting adjuncts. //19//
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone; therefore, you should also act, having regard for the maintenance of the world. 3.20
Śrīdhara: Here he cites the conduct of the virtuous as authoritative with the words "by action alone" (karmaṇaiva).
The meaning is that those whose inner being (sattva) has been purified by action alone have attained *saṃsiddhi*, which is perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Even though you consider yourself to be one who possesses perfect knowledge, [you have not yet attained it].

Nevertheless, he says "for the sake of the world's welfare" and so forth, [meaning] that the performance of action is indeed auspicious. "The gathering of the world" means setting it toward its own duty:
"When I perform action, all people will do likewise."
Otherwise, by using the example of the knower, the ignorant man would fall by abandoning his own duty, which is obligatory action;
thus, even considering the protection of the world as a purpose, how can you possibly act [otherwise]?
The meaning is that you should not abandon it. //20//
Madhusūdana:

Now, it is indeed ordained that even for one who merely desires knowledge (*vividiṣu*), there must be renunciation characterized by the abandonment of all ritual action (*sarva-karma-tyāga*) in order to practice hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) for the sake of attaining steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*).
Thus, it is not only the possessor of knowledge (*jñānin*) who lacks qualification for action, but also the seeker of knowledge who is dispassionate.

And thus, in order to dispel Arjuna’s doubt— that even one like me, being dispassionate and seeking knowledge, must surely abandon actions— the Blessed One refutes it by demonstrating that a Kṣatriya lacks the qualification for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) through the words "by action alone.
Janaka and others— Janaka, Jātaśatru, and so forth, who are renowned in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as learned Kṣatriyas—

even they, while engaged in action and not by abandoning action, attained *saṃsiddhi*, meaning they reached the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) which is accomplished through hearing [the scriptures] and other means.

Since this is so, therefore you too—whether a Kṣatriya desiring to know or one who already knows—ought to perform action; this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). For in the scriptural injunction prescribing renunciation—"A Brāhmaṇa, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then wanders about as a mendicant"—the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is intended to be significant, just as the status of being a Kṣatriya is [intended] in the statement, "A king desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya."
According to the Smṛti: "There are four stages of life for a Brāhmaṇa, three for a Kṣatriya, O King, and two for a Vaiśya. And in the Purāṇa as well:
"This dharma, which is the wearing of the marks of Viṣṇu, belongs to those born from the mouth [of Brahmā];
it is not praised as a dharma for those born from the arms or the thighs."
Thus, the absence of renunciation for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya has been stated.
Therefore, what was said by the Blessed One is indeed appropriate: "For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone";

and because of Smṛti texts such as "All duties are dependent on the king; the king is the upholder of dharma," he says [in the verse beginning with] "lokasaṅgraham" that a Kṣatriya must necessarily perform action even for the sake of maintaining the system of castes and stages of life.

The "gathering of the world" (*loka-saṅgraha*) consists in setting people upon their respective duties and turning them away from wrong paths; the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that even while observing this—and by the force of the word "even" (*api*), also observing the conduct of the wise such as Janaka—you ought indeed to perform action.

For you, whose body was commenced by action that brought about birth as a Kṣatriya, although you are a man of knowledge, [you must act] like Janaka and others due to the fruit of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma.
The intention is that you are fit to perform action for the sake of gathering people to yourself (*loka-saṅgraha*), but not to renounce it, because of the attainment of birth as a Brāhmaṇa.
It should be understood that the author of the *Bhāṣya*, knowing such an intention of the Blessed One, determined that renunciation belongs only to the Brāhmaṇa and not to others;
whereas the author of the *Vārttika* stated, merely as a bold assertion (*prauḍhi-vāda*), that renunciation exists even for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. //20//
Viśvanātha:
Here, he cites the conduct of the virtuous as authoritative with the words "by action.
Or, even if you consider yourself qualified for knowledge, [you must still act].
He says "in the world" (loke) to indicate that even for that [meditation], one should perform action itself for the sake of acquiring training in the world. //20//
Baladeva: Here he cites right conduct as the authority with the words "by action alone" (*karmaṇaiva*).
Having become pure-minded through the very means of action, they attained and established themselves in *saṃsiddhi*, characterized by the perception of their own Self.
The particle *eva* (alone), being connected specifically with the word "action," excludes its non-connection, just as in the expression "white as a conch shell" (*śaṅkha-pāṇḍura eva*).
Therefore, there is no exclusion of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.
Some maintain that [hearing] occurs together with ritual action (*karman*), such as sacrifice (*yajña*) and the like.
But has it not been stated that for one established in the higher stage (*saniṣṭha*), there is no performance of ritual action in the vision of the Self?
If it is asked, "How can there be an instruction on action for me, who have attained perfection and have beheld both myself and others?"—to that he says: "In the world...

It is true that you are indeed such [a perfected being]; nevertheless, perform action for the sake of sustaining the world (*loka-saṅgraha*). While I am performing action in Arjuna, the whole world will perform action. Otherwise, following my example, even ignorant people would abandon action and fall [into ruin]. Thus, the preservation of the world is the fruit of that [action]. //20//
Whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows that. (3.21)

Śrīdhara: He explains how the welfare of the world may be maintained through the performance of action with the words "That which... Even an ordinary person (itaraḥ prākṛtaḥ) performs that very same [action] which that superior person regards as authoritative—whether it be the scripture on action (karma-śāstra) or the scripture on its cessation (nivṛtti-śāstra).
The world also follows that very same path. //21//
Madhusūdana:

Anticipating the objection, "Even if I perform action, why should the world follow suit? he says, "Whatever [he does]," because people conform to the conduct of the superior. Whatever action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—the superior one, such as a king who is preeminent, performs, that very same action other ordinary people, following him, perform.
The meaning is that [the world acts] not independently in any other way.

Now, one might object: "Having observed the scriptures, why does the world not abandon non-scriptural excellent conduct and practice only that which is scriptural? Anticipating this doubt, the author shows that in the matter of both conduct and understanding, others follow the superior person by means of the words "sa yat" (when he...).

The meaning is this: whatever standard of authority—whether worldly or Vedic—he, as the best [of men], establishes and regards as authoritative, that very thing the world also follows and accepts as authoritative, rather than acting independently on anything of its own accord.

Thus, the intention is that you, the king, who are the primary figure, must certainly perform action for the sake of protecting the world, according to the maxim that "the conduct of people follows the lead of the principal."
Viśvanātha:
He explains the very method for the maintenance of the world with the words "whatever... (yad yad). //21//
Baladeva: He explains the manner of gathering the world precisely with the words "whatever [the best man does]":
whatever action the most excellent (śreṣṭha), the greatest (mahattama), performs, even the inferior (itara), the lesser one, performs in that very same way.
Whatever scripture the best man accepts as authoritative (pramāṇa) regarding that action, the world—the inferior one also—follows him and pursues that very same path.
The meaning is that the excellent conduct endowed with scriptural authority should be practiced by the younger brother who desires welfare.
In this way, any arbitrary behavior on the part of one who is powerful and superior is excluded;
for even though such behavior may be performed by a superior person, it lacks the quality of being endowed with scriptural authority. //21//
"O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by Me; nor is there anything unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action. (3.22)
Śrīdhara: Regarding this, he says "Not for Me" in three verses, stating that he himself is the very example here:
"O Pārtha, there is nothing to be done by Me."
Since there is nothing in the three worlds that has not been obtained, that has not been reached, yet remains to be obtained or attained;
nevertheless, the meaning is: "I am indeed engaged in action," that is, I simply perform action. //22//

Madhusūdana says, "In this matter, I myself am the very example," through three verses beginning with "na me. O Pārtha, for me there is nothing whatsoever that remains to be done in all the three worlds.
Since there is no fruit unattained by me that remains to be attained, nevertheless I continue in action; the meaning is that I perform action indeed.
By addressing him as "O Pārtha," he shows: "You, born of a pure Kṣatriya lineage and being the offspring of a hero, ought to conduct yourself exactly like me. //22//
Viśvanātha:
Here, he states in three verses that he himself is the very example. //22//

Baladeva: [The Lord] says "na me pārtha... (O Pārtha, for Me... in three verses to provide His own example for the purpose that even one who is the most excellent and independent of the fruits of action should perform the duties prescribed by the scriptures for the sake of maintaining worldly order (*loka-saṅgraha*).
For Me, the Lord of all, whose will is true and whose desires are true, there is nothing to be done;
indeed, action is to be performed only by one who seeks a fruit.
The meaning is that for Me—who am the very self of the supreme fruit and the locus of all fruits—no action is required.
He demonstrates this with the words "in the three.
Since there is no fruit whatsoever to be obtained through action in all the worlds that remains unobtained or unattained by Me; the meaning is that all of that is already Mine.
Nevertheless, he says "I act" (varte) to show that he indeed performs the action prescribed by the scriptures. //22//
For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly at any time, O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect. (3.23)

Śrīdhara: He shows the destruction of the world that would result from non-performance [of action] with the words "yadi hy aham" (if indeed I...). "Jātu" means at any time; "atandritaḥ" means being free from sloth; if I were not to engage in action—that is, if I were not to perform action—[the world would perish].
In that case, the meaning is that human beings follow my very path, or will follow it. //23//
Madhusūdana [says]:
Anticipating the objection that "you should not even engage in the maintenance of the world because it would be fruitless," he says, "If indeed I...
If, moreover, I, being untiring and free from laziness, were at any time (*jātu*)—that is, ever—to not engage in action, meaning I were not to perform it;
Then, O Pārtha, men who are entitled to perform action will follow—indeed, they shall follow in every way and in all respects—the path and way of Me, who am the Supreme Being. 23.
Viśvanātha:
"Anuvartate" means "they would continue to follow. //23//
Baladeva said: "If"— that is,

even though I am the Lord of all and have already accomplished every purpose, yet having descended into the Yadu clan, if I were ever (*jātu*) at any time not to abide in, or were not to perform, the duties prescribed by the scriptures and appropriate for that family, remaining vigilant and attentive (*atandritaḥ*), then let me be the example.
The meaning is that, having made me—the Supreme Being—follow the path consisting of the abandonment of family-prescribed conduct, men would follow it and thereby fall away from their duty. //23//
If I were not to perform action, these worlds would perish; I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings. (3.24)
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says, "utsīdeyuḥ" (they would perish).
They would perish—that is, they would be destroyed—through the neglect of dharma.
And therefore, whatever confusion of castes might arise, I alone would be its author;
in this way, I alone would destroy and defile the subjects. //24//
Madhusūdana:
It is indeed appropriate for men to follow the path of one who is supreme; yet, as to what fault there might be in such following, he says, "They would perish.

If I, the Lord, were not to perform action, then since even Manu and others who follow me would find action impossible, all these worlds would perish due to the disappearance of action, which is the cause of the world's maintenance.
They would perish;
and consequently, I alone would be the author of the intermingling of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*).
By that, I alone would bring ruin upon all these creatures and destroy them through the transgression of *dharma*.
And how could there be the intention, "I, being the Lord who has set out for the sake of favoring living beings, should destroy them all"?
Regarding the verse beginning with "Whatever he performs," there is another interpretation:
not only should you act because of the need to maintain the world, but also because of being a superior example; thus he says, "Whatever... and so forth.
And thus, the meaning is this: whatever my conduct as the superior is, that very same must be performed by you who follow me, and not something else independently.
In response to the inquiry, "Of what nature is your conduct which I should follow?", its demonstration is provided by the three verses beginning with "Not by me, O Pārtha" (2.21). //24//
Viśvanātha:

[If I were not to act,] those who do not practice Dharma would perish, taking me as their precedent; they would fall away from the path, and consequently, there would be a confusion of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*). I alone would be the cause of that as well, and thus I alone would destroy my subjects.
I shall make them pure. //24//
Baladeva says: To the question "What would happen then?", he replies with the words "they would perish.
If I, being the most excellent of all, do not perform the action prescribed by the scriptures, then these worlds would perish, meaning their moral boundaries (*maryādā*) would be destroyed.
When that destruction occurs, I alone would be the author of the resulting confusion (*saṅkara*).

And thus, as Prajāpati, I would defile these creatures with the fault of confusion and make them impure. Furthermore, even though Hari—who, despite teaching in this way, desires the happiness of His own devotees—has been seen to act according to His own will, He is celebrated by the Śruti as "this is the bridge, the support, for the non-confusion of these worlds," because He maintains the boundaries of the worlds; yet such a breach of those very boundaries would result from my doing so. Thus, even while instructing in this manner, whatever independent conduct was observed of Him who desired the welfare of His devotees—
Indeed, because it is not accompanied by the words of an injunction and because it belongs to the Lord, it must certainly not be performed by those who are inferior.
As it was said by the venerable Śuka:
"The word of the lords is true."
In some cases, one should likewise follow their conduct; a wise person should practice that which is consistent with their own words.
One who lacks mastery should never perform this even in thought; for by performing it out of delusion, one perishes.
"Just as Rudra [drank] the poison born from the ocean," so it is said. //24//
Just as the ignorant act with attachment to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world. 3.25

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he concludes that even one who knows the Self must perform action out of compassion for the sake of maintaining the world, by saying "the attached" (saktāḥ). Just as those who are unenlightened perform actions while being attached to and intent upon them, so too should the wise man, though unattached, act if he desires to maintain the world. //25//
Madhusūdana:
Now, for you, the Lord, who performs actions even while acting for the sake of the world's welfare, there is no harm whatsoever because of the absence of the conceit of agency (*kartṛtvābhimāna*).

But for me, a *jīva*, performing actions for the sake of the world's welfare, there would be an obscuration of knowledge due to the conceit of agency; therefore, he says: "The attached... [and so forth].

Just as the ignorant— those who are unenlightened and attached, being deeply involved in action through the conceit of agency and the desire for results— perform action, so too should the enlightened one, the knower of the Self, act even while desiring to maintain the world;
however, he should do so remaining unattached, meaning without performing the conceit of agency or the desire for results.

By the word "Bhārata," he shows that you are worthy of understanding the meaning of the aforementioned scriptures, either because you are born into the lineage of Bharata (bhara-ta-vaṃśodbhavatvena), or because you take delight (rata) in wisdom (jñāna). //25//
Viśvanātha:
Therefore, he concludes with the verse beginning "The attached," that even a man of knowledge who has attained firm stability must perform action. //25//

Baladeva: Therefore, with the intention that even though [the Self] is established [in its own nature], you should perform your own duty as declared in the Vedas for the benefit of the world, He says, "The attached...
Just as the ignorant act, being attached to action and intent upon the desire for results, so too should the wise man act;
however, he should do so being unattached, that is, free from the desire for results.
The rest is clear. //25//

The wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should not cause a confusion of intellect among the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them toward all works by performing them himself. 3.26

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Surely it would be more appropriate to instruct them in the knowledge of reality out of compassion. [Reply: No; he says "not causing confusion of intellect" (*na buddhi-bhedam*). Therefore, one should not produce a "confusion of intellect"—that is, a state of alteration—in those who are ignorant and consequently attached to action, by teaching that the Self is a non-agent.
One should not cause the intellect to waver away from its engagement with action.
Rather, he should encourage and practice them;
that is to say, he should cause the ignorant to perform their duties.
How? Being disciplined and attentive, while practicing them himself.
The sense is that if the intellect is caused to waver, there would be a loss of both [merit and knowledge] for them, because faith in ritual actions ceases and knowledge does not arise. //26//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might ask: what is the reason that the maintenance of the world must be accomplished through the performance of action alone, and not by the instruction of the knowledge of reality? To this he says, "Not [by] intellect... [referring to the verse beginning with *na buddhi-bhedaṃ janayet*].

For those who are ignorant, lacking discrimination, attached to action due to the conceit of agency and the desire for fruits, and who are deeply intent upon ritual action—[for them, the Lord does not cause confusion of intellect].
One should not effect a distinction or a displacement of that intellect which thinks, "I shall perform this action" and "I shall enjoy this fruit," by means of the teaching of a non-agent self.

Rather, being disciplined and attentive, the wise man, desiring to maintain the world order, should practice all actions pertaining to the domain of the ignorant; having generated faith in them, he should cause them to rejoice with pleasure.
One should serve [the teacher].

For if one causes the intellect of those who lack qualification to waver by giving them instruction, there would result a state of falling away from both, due to the cessation of faith in ritual actions and the non-arising of knowledge.
And so it has been said:
"He who says 'everything is Brahman' to one who is ignorant or only half-awakened is thereby cast into the snares of the great hells. (26)
Viśvanātha:

Enough with this dullness regarding action! One should not create a division in the intellect by thinking, "Having renounced action, you shall achieve your purpose through the practice of knowledge just as I have," toward those who are attached to action and whose internal organs are unpurified, for they possess attachment to actions alone.
But you, seeking to achieve your goal, should engage in and cause others to perform actions solely as desireless action (niṣkāma-karma).
In this regard, while performing actions yourself, you should serve as an example.
Now, [one might ask]:

This contradicts the words of Ajita: "One who knows the supreme good himself does not perform action for one who is ignorant; for even the best of physicians does not give unwholesome food to a patient, even if he desires it. (BhP 6.9.5)
True;
however, there is no contradiction, for that [previous statement] concerns one who teaches through devotion (*bhakti*), whereas this concerns one who teaches through knowledge (*jñāna*),
since knowledge is dependent upon the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
For that [liberation] depends upon desireless action for its purification,
whereas devotion is inherently powerful and does not require the purification of the internal organ as a prerequisite; therefore,
if one is able to generate faith in devotion, [that is sufficient].

At that time, it might even cause a division in the intellect of those engaged in ritual action, because those possessed of faith in devotion have no further qualification for ritual action; therefore,
one should perform rituals as long as one does not become weary of them.
"Or as long as faith does not arise from hearing my stories and so forth" (BhP 11.20.9);
"He who, having abandoned all duties, worships me, is indeed the best of beings" (BhP 11.11.32);
and "Having renounced all duties, take refuge in me alone" (Gītā 18.66).
Having abandoned his own duty, if one who is immature worships the lotus feet of Hari and should then fall from that state... [BhP 1.5.17]
This should be analyzed based on such statements as these. //26//
Baladeva: Furthermore, one who desires the welfare of the world and possesses knowledge should be vigilant; thus he says, "Not [causing] confusion of intellect" (*na buddhi-bhedaṃ*).

Even a learned man who is firmly established in realization should not cause a confusion of intellect among the ignorant—those attached to action and possessed by the dullness born of faith in ritual acts. The meaning is that he should not divert them from their devotion to action by saying, "Like me, you shall achieve your purpose through knowledge alone. He should not cause them to abandon their mental resolve toward the path of action.

But one who is himself engaged in actions, being vigilant and performing them all properly with the integration of every limb, should cause all prescribed duties to shine forth—that is, he should serve them with love and cause ignorant people to perform those actions;
this is the meaning.
The sense is that if there were a division of intellect, faith in actions would cease and knowledge would not arise, whereby they would become "fallen from both."
"One who knows the supreme good himself does not perform action for one who is ignorant;
for even the best of physicians does not prescribe unwholesome food to a patient, even if that patient desires it.
This statement by Ajita (Uddhava) should be understood as being directed toward those who are attached to and devoted to ritual action. (26)
All actions performed in every way by the qualities of material nature, one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. (3.27)
Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "If even the wise person must perform action, then what is the distinction between the wise and the ignorant?
Anticipating this doubt, he shows the distinction between the two with the following two verses beginning with *prakṛteḥ*.
"By the qualities of nature"—that is, by the senses, which are the effects of nature—actions are performed in every way.
He thinks, "I alone am the agent; I am doing these things.
The reason for this is that his intellect is deluded by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), through which he superimposes the self upon the senses and other faculties. //27//
Madhusūdana:

Although there is equality between the wise and the ignorant regarding the performance of action, he elucidates the meaning of the verse beginning with "Attached to action... by means of two verses starting with "From nature...", demonstrating the distinction between them based on the presence or absence of the conceit of agency.

*Prakṛti* is *māyā*, consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, whose nature is false knowledge; it is the supreme power of the Lord, according to the Vedic scripture: "One should know *māyā* as *prakṛti*, and the Great Lord as the wielder of *māyā*. By the qualities of that *prakṛti*—that is, by its modifications in the form of effects and causes—all actions, both worldly and Vedic, are performed in every way through the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is the notion of selfhood with respect to the aggregate of cause and effect.
One whose inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is deluded—meaning an Ātman incapable of discriminating its own true nature—is one whose self is deluded by egoism (ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā).
Such a person, identifying the Self with what is not the Self, conceives through the superimposition of agency that "I am the doer" and "I am performing these actions.
The suffix *tṛn* in the word "kartāham" (I am the doer) denotes the present tense.
Therefore, by the rule *tena na lokāvyaya-niṣṭhā-khal-artha-tṛṇām* (Pāṇini 2.3.69), there is a prohibition of the genitive case. //27//
Viśvanātha:
Now, if even a man of knowledge should perform action, then what is the distinction between the man of knowledge and the ignorant man?
Anticipating this doubt, he shows the distinction between the two with the following two verses: "Of nature... [27].
An ignorant person thinks, "I alone am the agent; I perform those actions which are being performed in every way—that is, by all means—by the qualities of nature, that is, by the senses."
Baladeva: Even though there is equality in being an agent, he states the distinction between the wise and the ignorant in two verses beginning with "prakṛteḥ.
A person whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer of actions.

The prohibition of the genitive case [in the compound *lokāvyayanisthā*] follows from the sūtra: "The genitive is not used [with a word denoting the object of an action] when it expresses a state that is eternal in the world" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.69).
Actions are both worldly and Vedic.

To the question of what kind they are, he says: they are performed by means of the qualities (*guṇa*) of *prakṛti*—that is, by its effects, the body, senses, and vital breaths—which are set in motion by the Lord.

This alone must be understood from the determination at the outset: that the individual self (*jīvātman*), whose nature is consciousness, who is the object of our concern, and who is the agent, is overwhelmed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoying objects throughout beginningless time.

Embracing his own nature which is present for the sake of experiencing those objects, his self deluded by the egoism (ahaṅkāra) that is the effect thereof, devoid of such true self-knowledge, and possessing the sense of "I" with respect to the body and so forth, he thinks: "The actions accomplished through the body and other means, as well as by the Lord, were performed by me alone."
The agency that belongs to the self as agent is indeed established through three factors— the body and so forth, the supreme self, and the universal impeller—
and not by the individual soul alone.

And that which the individual soul (jīva) thinks, "This is accomplished by me alone," arises solely from the delusion of egoism (*ahaṅkāra-vimauḍhya*). This is because of the three verses at the end of the final chapter beginning with, "The Lord is the supervisor, and likewise... (Gītā 18.14). Furthermore, regarding what will be described in the passage, "In the state of being the agent of cause and effect, nature (*prakṛti*) is said to be the cause" (Gītā 13.18)—wherein the agency over the body, senses, and so forth is attributed to nature—that agency cannot be understood as belonging to nature alone.
Since it is accepted that its activity occurs only through association with a person (puruṣa), it will be explained that the agency of the person is therefore unavoidable. //27//

But he who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the distinction between the qualities and their functions, does not become attached, realizing that "it is the qualities acting upon the qualities. (3.28)
Śrīdhara says: "But the wise man does not think thus," and so he says, "one who knows the truth.
"I am not of the nature of the qualities" (guṇātmaka) signifies the self's distinction from the qualities; "actions are not mine" signifies the self's distinction even from actions.
He who knows the true nature of that division between the qualities (guṇas) and actions does not harbor the persistent attachment to agency.
The reason for this is stated as "the qualities":
having realized that the qualities—the senses—operate upon the qualities—the objects—and that "I am not" [the agent], he remains free from such attachment. //28//
Madhusūdana says that the wise man, however, does not think in that way; thus he says, "the knower of reality" (tattvavit).
One who knows reality—that is, the true nature (yāthātmya)—is a knower of reality.
By the word "tu" (but), he states its distinction from ignorance.
To the question "Of what [is this the reality]?", he says: "of the division between the qualities and actions.

Here, "qualities" (guṇas) refers to the body, the senses, and the internal organs, which are the substrata of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); and "actions" (karmāṇi) refers to their activities, which are the substrata of the sense of "mine" (mama-kāra). Thus, "guṇa-karma" is a copulative compound (dvandva) treated as a singular.
*Vibhāga* (division) is that which is distinguished as the illuminator of all insentient, mutable things; it is the Self (*ātman*), whose nature is self-luminous knowledge and which is unattached.

*Guṇa-karma-vibhāgaḥ* is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) meaning "qualities, actions, and division. Of those two—the division of qualities and actions, and the division of the illuminated and the illuminator, or the insentient and the conscious, the mutable and the immutable—...

He who knows reality— true nature— does not become attached; thinking that the *guṇas*, which consist of the instruments of action, operate upon the *guṇas* as objects because they are subject to modification,
whereas the Self is changeless, he does not form an attachment— that is, he does not harbor the misconception of agency like one who does not know reality,
O mighty-armed one.

Thus, by addressing him in this way, he indicates that because you possess the characteristics of a "true person" (satpuruṣa) as described in the *Sāmudrika* [treatise], you ought not to be undiscriminating like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Alternatively, it means "one who knows the reality of the division of the qualities (*guṇa*) and the division of actions (*karman*).

In this latter case, since the sense could be established by the words "of the qualities and actions" (*guṇakarmaṇoḥ*) alone, the purpose of including the word "division" (*vibhāga*) must be considered. //28//
Viśvanātha:
He is one who knows the true nature (*tattva*) of those two divisions, namely of the qualities (*guṇa*) and of action (*karman*).
Among these, the division of qualities consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The classification of karma consists of the distinctions among the effects such as sentient beings, deities, sense faculties, and their objects;
the reality of these two refers to their essential nature,
and one who knows that is a knower of reality.
The qualities are the presiding deities; the senses, such as the eye and others, are to be employed, and they operate upon the objects which are the qualities, such as form and so forth.
But I am neither a quality nor anything that is an effect of the qualities.
Nor is there any connection of mine with those qualities or the effects of those qualities; thinking thus, the wise man does not become attached. //28//
Baladeva says: "But the knower [of truth] is not so," thus he states "the knower of reality" (*tattva-vit*).

One who knows the reality of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the distinction between actions—that is, the reality which is the essential nature of the self's own differentiation and separation from the *guṇas*, namely the senses, and from the actions performed by them—through the thorough investigation of their respective differences, does not [identify with them]. Thus: "I am not... [he says].
The meaning is that he knows [the Self] as having qualities, actions, and form.
For those qualities are the senses; impelled by their respective deities, they operate upon objects such as sound and so forth, and they manifest them.
But I am distinct from them, because I consist of unattached consciousness and bliss.
Thinking, "I do not exist within them in that form, nor do I manifest them," they do not become attached to them;
rather, they become attached only to the Self.
Here too, by the word "having thought" (matvā), it should be understood that agency is attributed to the individual soul (jīva). //28//
Those who are deluded by the qualities of material nature become attached to the actions of those qualities;
one who knows the whole should not disturb those dull-witted people who do not know the whole. 3.29
Śrīdhara: He concludes [the teaching] with the words "not causing a division of intellect" by saying "of nature" (*prakṛteḥ*).
Those who, being utterly deluded by the qualities (*guṇa*) of nature—namely *sattva* and the others—become attached to the qualities, that is, to the senses and their functions;
the knower of the whole, the omniscient one, should not cause those limited knowers, the dull-witted ones, to waver. (29)
Madhusūdana:

Thus, having stated that because the performance of action is the same for both the knower and the ignorant, the knower should not cause a disturbance in the intellect of the ignorant, he concludes [the section]:
those who are thoroughly deluded by the qualities (*guṇa*) of *prakṛti*—that is, by the aforementioned *māyā*—which manifest as effects such as the body and other transformations.

Those who, due to the non-manifestation of their true nature, consider those very things [the body, senses, and mind] to be the Self, and who— thinking "we shall perform attachment for the sake of the fruits of these very qualities, namely the body, senses, and internal organ"— become attached to their activities and operations, forming a very firm sense of ownership;
those who are thus attached to action, who know the Self incompletely, who identify with the non-Self, and who are intoxicated by pride because of their impure minds— [I speak of them].

The meaning is that one who knows all and is a knower of the perfected Self should not himself unsettle those who have not yet attained the qualification for knowledge; that is, he should not cause them to fall away from their faith in action.

However, the intention is that those whose internal organs are not dull and are pure move forward by themselves through the arising of discernment once they have attained the qualification for knowledge.

The terms "entire" (*kṛtsna*) and "non-entire" (*akṛtsna*) have been explained by the authors of the Vārttika as referring respectively to the Self (*ātman*) and the non-Self (*anātman*), in accordance with the meaning of the Śruti:

"Since the entire reality is non-dual on account of such statements as 'Being alone,' whence could there be the possibility of a non-entire object that is its opposite? (*sad evety ādi-vākyebhyaḥ kṛtsnaṃ vastu yato 'dvayam / sambhavas tad-viruddhasya kuto 'kṛtsnasya vastunaḥ //*).
"When an object is seen, that which is not seen remains as something other than it;

likewise, when it is unseen, that which is seen would remain. Such a thing is called incomplete. Thus, because the non-self (anātman) possesses parts and possesses manifold properties, it is [only partially] perceived through some property or some part.
Even when that one particular object, such as a jar, is known, that very same object remains unknown as qualified by other properties or other parts; furthermore,
other things such as a cloth remain unknown as well.

Likewise, even when that jar or other object is unknown, a cloth or other thing might be known; and even when that [jar] is known, because there is ignorance of another, and when it is unknown, because there is knowledge of another, it is called "incomplete.
However, the Absolute (kṛtsna) is the non-dual Self alone, because when that is known, there is no remainder whatsoever—this is the meaning of the two verses. //29//
Viśvanātha:

Now, if individual souls (*jīva*) are distinct from the *guṇas* and the effects of the *guṇas*, and are therefore unconnected to them, then how is it that they are seen to become attached to sense objects?
To this he replies: "Deluded by the *guṇas* of *prakṛti*, and having attained delusion through absorption in them"—just as a man possessed by a spirit considers himself to be that very spirit.
In the same way, individual souls (jīvas) possessed by the qualities of nature (prakṛti-guṇas) consider themselves to be those very qualities;
consequently, they become attached to the actions of the qualities—that is, to sense objects which are the effects of the qualities.
One who knows everything (kṛtsnavit), the omniscient one, should not cause those of dull intellect, who do not know the whole truth, to waver from that state.

One does not strive to bring about the realization that "you are the individual soul (jīva) distinct from the qualities (guṇas), and not the quality itself," but rather causes one to perform desireless action (niṣkāma-karma) which removes the possession by the qualities.
For a person possessed by a spirit does not regain his health even through a hundred instructions saying, "You are not the spirit, but you are indeed a human being."
However, the intended meaning is that [the afflictions are removed] solely through the application of medicines, jewels, mantras, and so forth, which serve as their antidotes. //29//
Baladeva: He concludes with the words "prakṛteḥ" (of nature), stating that one should not cause a disturbance in their understanding.

Deluded by the quality (*guṇa*) of nature—that is, by its effect, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)—people, according to the analogy of being possessed by a spirit, consider the body and so forth to be the self; they become attached to the activities, the functions, of the *guṇas*, namely the body and the senses.

One who knows the whole—the possessor of full knowledge of the Self—should not unsettle those of limited vision, the small-minded, the dull-witted, who are lazy in grasping the reality of the Self. You are one who knows the whole, distinct from the qualities and their actions, and consisting of pure consciousness and bliss.

The intention is this: one should not desire to make [the disciple] grasp the truth in this manner, but rather, following his inclination, one should desire to make him inclined toward the reality of the Self by means of a gradual progression through Vedic rituals. //29//
Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self, free from desire and free from the sense of "mine," fight, devoid of feverish anxiety. (3.30)
Śrīdhara: Thus, even for one who knows the truth, action must be performed.
But you are not yet a knower of the truth;
therefore, he says "in Me" (mayi), meaning: perform only action.
Having renounced all actions by surrendering them unto Me—
with an inward-turned mind, through the vision that "I perform action dependent upon the Inner Ruler"—
and being free from desire, devoid of longing.

Therefore, having become free from the sense of "mine" by thinking, "This action for the sake of Me is the means to attain My fruit," and having become free from fever and abandoned grief, [perform your duty]. //30//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, although there is equality in the performance of action, a distinction has been stated based on the ignorant and the wise having, respectively, an attachment to agency and its absence. Now, by stating that even for the ignorant seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is a distinction—namely, the offering of actions to the Lord and the absence of desire for fruits—in comparison with one who does not seek liberation, [the Lord] confirms Arjuna’s entitlement to action on account of his ignorance.

"In me" means: in me—the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, the omniscient, the controller of all, the Self of all—one should offer all actions, both worldly and Vedic, in every manner, with a mind directed toward the inner self, thinking: "I am the agent, yet dependent upon the Inner Controller. Therefore...
Having renounced and surrendered all actions with the understanding, "I perform these works for the Lord, as a servant does for a king," one should be free from expectations,
devoid of desire, and free from the sense of "mine" (*nirmama*)— meaning empty of possessiveness toward one's own body, children, brothers, and so forth— and thus be without fever.
By the word "fever" (*jvara*), grief itself is meant, because it is the cause of distress.

The intention is this: having become free from sorrow caused by ill repute in this world or the next, or by falling into hell, you, as one desiring liberation, should fight—that is, perform the actions prescribed for you.
In this regard, offering all actions to the Blessed One and being free from desire are common requirements for every action of one who seeks liberation.

It should be understood that freedom from possessiveness and the abandonment of grief apply specifically to the context of battle alone, because possessiveness and grief do not otherwise arise [in that specific context]. //30//
Viśvanātha:
Therefore, "in me" means "in the self by means of the mind directed toward the inner self (*adhyātma-cetasā*). Thus, *adhyātmam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva-samāsa*).

And therefore, that mind which is directed toward the Self is the "inward-turned mind" (*adhyātma-cetas*); by such a mind—one fixed solely on the Self, and not one fixed on sense objects—having renounced or surrendered all actions unto Me, fight without desire for reward (*nirāśīḥ*), free from longing (*niṣkāma*), and devoid of the sense of "mine-ness" (*nirmama*) regarding everything. //30//

Baladeva: Because it is so— "in Me"— therefore, being firmly established through the knowledge whose object is the reality of your own Self, which is the inner self (*adhyātma*), renounce all actions by surrendering them to Me, the Supreme Lord, like a servant to a king, and fight.
Free from the attachment to being an agent,
just as a servant under a king's authority performs his duties by the king's command, so too you, who are under my authority and desire to sustain the worlds, perform those actions by my command.
The mind directed toward the self is "inner-directed mind" (*adhyātma-cetas*);
[this is a compound] in the sense of a case ending (*vibhakty-artha*). Being "free from desire" means being devoid of the wish for its fruit, thinking: "I act by the command of my Master."
Therefore, being free from the sense of "mine" by realizing that these actions are for My sake and are the means to attain Me as the fruit;
and having become free from fever— that is, having abandoned the distress caused by the slaughter of kinsmen—
it was said to Arjuna, "Fight," because of his status as a Kṣatriya.
The meaning of the statement is that those seeking liberation must perform the duties prescribed for their own stage of life (āśrama). //30//
Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and free from cavil, they too are liberated from the bonds of action. (3.31)

Śrīdhara: Thus, he states the merit in the performance of action with the words "Those who... Those who have faith in my word, and who, not finding fault—that is, not perceiving defects in the thought that it impels one toward action which is essentially suffering—follow this, my teaching, they too, performing action gradually, [attain] perfect...
Like those possessing knowledge, they are liberated from karmas. //31//
Madhusūdana says:

"The performance of prescribed duties with the intention of offering them to the Lord, free from any desire for fruits, results in liberation through the purification of the mind and the attainment of knowledge;
this is what [the Lord] expresses in the words 'ye me'."

This is my teaching: the performance of prescribed duties without attachment to their fruits. It is "eternal" because it has been known through the eternal Vedas and has come down through an unbroken tradition; or it is "always necessary," meaning at all times. "Mānavāḥ" refers to human beings, since only humans have the qualification for ritual action. "Śraddhāvantaḥ" means those who possess faith—faith being the conviction that "it is exactly so," even regarding matters taught by the scriptures and teachers that have not yet been personally experienced.
Those who possess such qualities;

"envy" (asūyā) is the revelation of faults in [others'] virtues. And that [envy], in the present context, takes the form: "This person is merciless, since he is impelling me toward action which consists of suffering. This is what is relevant here.

Those who do not harbor such malice toward me, their guru Vāsudeva, the friend of all, and instead follow my teaching, they too— by means of the purification of the mind and the attainment of knowledge—
are liberated from actions known as dharma and adharma, just like those possessed of perfect knowledge. //31//
Viśvanātha says:
In order to encourage [the reader] to engage with his own composed instruction, he says, "Those who... (verse 31).
Baladeva: By stating the fruit for those who follow his own doctrine within the secret of the Śruti, he reveals its preeminence with the words "ye me" (those who [follow] Me).
"Nityam" means always, or as obtained from time immemorial because it is taught by the Śruti. "Śraddhāvantaḥ" means possessing firm conviction.

"Those who are free from the attribution of faults, thinking: 'Why this fruitless labor involving great exertion toward one who possesses the quality of being a liberator?'—the word 'api' (even/also) here functions as an emphasis. Alternatively, it refers to those who follow my teaching, as well as those who, though unable to practice it, possess faith in it."
The meaning is that even those who possess faith do not find fault with it.

The sense is that although they lack its actual practice at present, because their defects have been diminished through faith and by being free from malice toward it, they will eventually practice it to some extent and thereby be liberated. //31//
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded in all knowledge, lost, and devoid of sense. (32)
Śrīdhara: He states the fault in the contrary case with the words "But those who... (ye tv etad).

Know that those who do not practice this are mindless (*acetasaḥ*), devoid of discrimination; therefore, they are utterly deluded regarding all action as well as the knowledge concerning Brahman, and are thus ruined. //32//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus stated the merit in the case of conformity, he speaks of the defect in the case of deviation with the words "But those who...
The word "but" (tu) indicates a lack of faith, which is the opposite of faith.
Therefore, those who, out of atheism, lack faith, are envious, and point out faults— those who do not follow this teaching of Mine;

such mindless ones of wicked heart, and for that very reason deluded regarding all knowledge, being confused about the various forms of knowledge concerning action, Brahman with attributes, and Brahman without attributes, in terms of their means of proof (*pramāṇa*), their objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and their purpose (*prayojana*).
Know—understand—that those who are in every way unfit are ruined and have fallen away from all goals of human endeavor. //32//
Viśvanātha:
He states the defect in the opposing view with the words "ye tu" (but those who...).
Baladeva: He states the defect in the opposing view with the words "ye tv etat" (but those who this...).

But know those who do not practice them to be senseless and devoid of discrimination; therefore, they are utterly deluded regarding all action as well as the knowledge concerning Brahman, and are ruined. //32//
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature; all beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish? (3.33)
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, since it yields great fruit, why do all people not restrain their senses and, being free from desire, practice only their own duty (svadharma)?
To this he says: *sadṛśam*.
*Prakṛti* is one's inherent nature (*svabhāva*), which is dependent upon the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of past actions.
Even one who possesses knowledge of virtues and defects acts only in accordance with, that is, in conformity to, their own respective nature or disposition;
what need is there to mention that an ignorant person acts so?
For all living beings, indeed, follow their own nature.
And this being so, what will the restraint of the senses accomplish?
The meaning is: because of the superior strength of primordial nature (prakṛti). //33//
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: Seeing that there is fear in transgressing your command just as there is for a king, why do they not follow your opinion even while being envious, or how is it that they become adverse toward the means for accomplishing all human goals?
To this, he says: "In accordance with their own nature" (sadṛśam).

What is called "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of dharma, adharma, knowledge, desire, and so forth, performed in a previous birth, which becomes manifest in the present life and is powerful in every respect. This is established by the scriptural authority: "Knowledge and action, as well as past experience (*pūrva-prajñā*), take hold of [the soul]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). According to the principle that "every living being—even one possessing knowledge or a knower of Brahman—is not distinct from beasts and the like," every creature acts in a manner strictly corresponding to and conforming with its own nature.
If even one who possesses knowledge of virtues and faults acts [thus], how much more so a fool?
Therefore, all beings—all living creatures—follow their own nature and return to it, even though that nature is the cause of the ruin of human purpose.
In that case, what will my restraint or the king's restraint accomplish?
The meaning is that one is unable to turn back from misdeeds due to the intensity of passion.

The underlying sense is that even though they know these acts lead to the great hells, people proceed toward sins because of the strength of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*), and thus they do not fear the fault of transgressing my command. //3.33//
Viśvanātha:
But surely, just as for a king, do those who do not follow the will of you, the Supreme Lord, not tremble at the punishment meted out by you, just as they would at one inflicted by a king? True;
however, this applies only to those who indeed continue to set their senses in motion.
Even those who possess discernment are unable to disregard the command of the king and of the Supreme Lord;
for it was their very nature to be thus, as he says with the word "similarly.
Even one possessed of knowledge, when such an evil deed has been committed, thinks: "In this way there will surely be hell, and in this way there will be punishment from the king."

Thinking, "In this way, ill-repute will arise," even one possessed of discrimination acts in a manner consistent with and appropriate to his own nature—the burden of suffering born from long-standing habituation to sin.

Therefore, they follow their *prakṛti*, which is their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). In that regard, restraint is effected—either by Me through My scriptures or by the King—so as to purify those of impure mind by means of the aforementioned Karma-yoga free from desire, and to purify those of pure mind by means of Jñāna-yoga.

And while He is able to awaken those whose minds are not utterly impure, He alone— through the yoga of devotion arising from His own spontaneous grace— is capable of uplifting even those of most sinful nature.
As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O divine sage, how fortunate you are, by whose grace even a lowly hunter, his hair standing on end with joy, has in an instant attained delight! (33)

Baladeva said: "Indeed, the scripture declares that punishment is ordained for those who transgress the will of the Lord of All; therefore, why do they not fear You? To this he replies with the words "sadṛśam" (in accordance). Even a person possessing knowledge—who understands the punishment prescribed in the scriptures—acts and proceeds in a manner that is "similar," meaning exactly conforming to his own innate tendencies (*prakṛti*), which are his own deep-seated impressions (*durvāsanā*) operating since beginningless time; how much more so, then, one who lacks such knowledge?

Consequently, all beings—everyone—follow that *prakṛti*, which is the cause of the ruin of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). In this regard, what will punishment—even one involving knowledge of the scriptures—accomplish for one who is devoid of association with the virtuous? The meaning is that it will not be able to turn back the power of the latent impressions (*durvāsanā*).

But for one who is accompanied by association with the virtuous, that [suffering], even if powerful, is destroyed; for according to such Smṛti texts as, "Only the virtuous sever his mental affliction through their words" (BhP 11.26.26). //33//
Attachment and aversion are established toward the objects of each sense organ. One should not come under their sway, for they are one's adversaries. (3.34)

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that if the activity of the *puruṣa* is thus dependent solely upon *prakṛti*, then the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would become useless. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of each and every sense-organ" (*indriyasyendriyasya*), using the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) to indicate that this applies to every single sense-organ individually.

Regarding their respective objects (*arthe*), namely their own specific domains, attachment (*rāga*) toward what is favorable and aversion (*dveṣa*) toward what is unfavorable—thus, attachment and aversion are "established," meaning they are necessarily present.
And thus, activity conforming to that [nature] is the inherent nature (*prakṛti*) of beings;
nevertheless, it is regulated by the scripture so that one should not remain subject to those two,
for (hi) because:
For this seeker of liberation, these two are adversaries and opposing forces.

The meaning is this: through the recollection of sense objects and so forth, passion and aversion are produced, and Nature forcibly impels the inattentive person toward misfortune, like a very deep current.
However, the scripture impels him even before that toward the worship of the Supreme Lord and other such practices which serve as obstacles to passion and aversion regarding sense objects.
